title: A-B-C of vegetable gardening
needIt: A simple small-garden manual a beginner can follow in one season.

chapters.title: Foreword

passages.old: OT everybody has a garden. Some deny themselves the pleasure and the profit of one because they have never had any experience in gardening, and have somehow got the impression that special training is necessary to make a success of the undertaking. Here is where they make a mistake. There is no special "'knack'"' about it. Any one who owns a bit of land, and has some time that can be given to garden-work, and an inclination to do so, can make a gardener of himself in a season, and a successful one, too, if he allows himself to be governed by the advice of some one who has had some experience along this line.
passages.plain: Not everyone has a garden. Some people do not have a garden because they have no experience. They think they need special training to succeed. They are wrong. Gardening does not require a special talent. Anyone who owns land and has time to work in a garden can become a gardener in one season. You can also be a successful gardener. You just need to follow the advice of someone who has experience.

passages.old: After the first season he will not be likely to ask or need advice, for the practical knowledge which comes with one season's work among vegetables will not only be sufficient to enable him to go on with his gardening operations on his own responsibility, but it will have made him so enthusiastic over them that he will be eager to enlarge his knowledge of "'the green things growing,' and in doing this he will find a pleasure that will make him wonder how he ever came to consider gardening something to dread.
passages.plain: After the first season, you will likely not need to ask for advice. The practical knowledge you gain from one season of working with vegetables will be enough for you to manage your garden on your own. This work will also make you very enthusiastic. You will want to learn more about growing plants. You will find so much pleasure in this that you will wonder why you ever thought gardening was something to fear.

passages.old: Others, who have but a small piece of land, may think it not worth while to attempt to grow vegetables on it. They labor under the impression that a garden, in order to prove a success, requires more land than is at their © disposal. Here is where they make a mistake. Of course one cannot grow a large quantity of vegetables on a small piece of ground, but the one who undertakes to make the most of a small piece will be surprised at the amount that can be grown on it.
passages.plain: Some people have only a small piece of land. They might think it is not worth trying to grow vegetables there. They believe a garden needs more land than they have to be successful. They are wrong. You cannot grow a huge amount of vegetables on a small piece of ground. However, if you try to make the most of a small piece, you will be surprised by how much you can grow on it.

passages.old: In a garden that is not more than twenty-five feet square a friend of mine grows all the summer vegetables required by his family of four persons. This calls for what the scientific people call 'Gntensive gardening,' and makes it necessary to plant and plan for a succession of vegetables; but that twenty-five feet square of ground enables him to get a good share of the summer living of his family. Another notion is, that in order to have a good garden a large amount of time and labor must be expended on it.
passages.plain: A friend of mine grows all the summer vegetables for his family of four in a garden that is no more than twenty-five feet square. This method is called intensive gardening. It requires you to plan and plant a succession of vegetables. This small area of ground allows him to grow a good share of his family's summer food. Some people think you must spend a large amount of time and labor to have a good garden.

passages.old: Not so. A very small amount of systematized labor will be demanded by even a good-sized garden, if it is planned in such a manner that labor-saving tools can be used in its cultivation. If we look back to the gardening days of fifty or even twenty-five years ago, when everything was done at the hardest and the hand had to do a good share of the work that we now do with helpful implements, it is not to be wondered at that the old-time care of a garden discourages many from undertaking to have one. - Happily those days are over, and with the gardening facilities of the present it is an easy matter to accomplish more in an hour than could be done then ina day.
passages.plain: That is not true. A large garden does not require much organized work if you plan it so that you can use tools that save labor. Many years ago, people did everything by hand. They did much of the work that we now do with helpful tools. It is no surprise that the hard work of the past stops many people from starting a garden. Those days are over now. With today's gardening tools, you can do more in one hour than people could do in a whole day back then.

passages.old: There is really no drudgery in gardening as it is done to-day. On the contrary, there is positive pleasure in the operation of the machinery which inventive genius has furnished for the up-to-date gardener's use. Those who have never had a garden of their own, but have bought vegetables in the ordinary market, are not in a position to understand the wide difference between the article we buy and the one which is taken directly from the ground and eaten at once. While it is possible to keep most vegetables looking fresh for a considerable time by the use of water and ice, it is not possible to make them retain that delicacy of flavor known only to those whose vegetables go straight from the garden to the kitchen.
passages.plain: Gardening is not boring today. You can actually enjoy using the modern machines that people have invented for gardeners. If you have never had your own garden and only buy vegetables at a market, you do not know the big difference between those vegetables and ones you pick from the ground to eat right away. You can keep most vegetables looking fresh for a long time using water and ice. However, you cannot make them keep the delicate flavor that only people who take vegetables straight from the garden to the kitchen know.

passages.old: If you want any vegetable at its best you must grow it in your own gurden. The general impression seems to be that gardening is essentially man's work, and that women and children are not equal to it. This is another mistake that will rapidly be done away with, for the woman of to-day is no longer a housed-up woman. She is rapidly learning the value of fresh air, and the tonic of outdoor life is fast taking the place of the doctor's prescriptions. 'The writer knows of many women who have found work in the garden not only a healthful occupation, but one so delightful that they look forward to spring with most pleasurable anticipations, and long for the time to come when they can get to work out of doors.
passages.plain: You must grow your own vegetables in your own garden if you want them to be at their best. Many people think that gardening is only for men. They think women and children are not good at it. This is a mistake that will soon disappear. Today's women are no longer stuck inside the house. They are learning that fresh air is valuable. Outdoor life is replacing doctor's prescriptions. The writer knows many women who find garden work healthy. They also find it so delightful that they look forward to spring with pleasure. They long for the time when they can work outside.

passages.old: When we have tried both we learn that work in the vegetable-garden is no harder than that in the flower-garden, and that neither demands more strength or time than the average woman is able to give it if she makes use of labor-saving tools. What is true of the woman is equally true of the children. A child ten years of age can do a good deal of the work that a good-sized garden calls for. I would not be understood as advocating the giving up of garden-work to women and children.
passages.plain: You will learn that working in a vegetable garden is not harder than working in a flower garden. Neither garden requires more strength or time than an average woman can give. She can do this work if she uses tools that save labor. This is also true for children. A child who is ten years old can do a lot of the work that a large garden needs. I am not saying that you should let women and children stop doing garden work.

passages.old: I would not deny man the pleasure of sharing in it. But I would urge the importance of interesting women and children in it, and of encouraging them to take part in it from the viewpoint of health. Benefit in other respects will become so apparent, after a little, that further encouragement will not be necessary. Most women who have some leisure, especially if they are of the housewife class, will be so pleased with the results of gardening that they will be glad to supplement the labors of the man of the family by what they -can accomplish in it, if he is employed in work that will not allow him to devote much time to the garden.
passages.plain: You should let men enjoy gardening. You should also encourage women and children to join in for their health. Other benefits will become clear quickly. After that, you will not need to encourage them anymore. Most women with free time, especially housewives, will be happy with the results of gardening. They will want to help the man of the family with the work. They will do this if he has a job that does not give him much time for the garden.

passages.old: And they will find that the boys of the family, and the girls as well, can be made to take an active part in the good work with but little encouragement from their elders. It is natural for both boys and girls to dig in the soil, and it is well to encourage them to dig A-B-C OF VEGETABLE GARDENING ~ to some purpose. It is natural work, and healthy work, and work that will do more to keep the average child out of mischief than any other influence that can be brought to bear on it.
passages.plain: You will find that the boys and girls in your family can take part in this good work. They only need a little encouragement from their elders. It is natural for both boys and girls to dig in the soil. You should encourage them to dig for a specific purpose. It is natural work and healthy work. This work will do more to keep the average child out of mischief than any other influence.

passages.old: But I would not allow the child. to get the impression that I gave it gardenwork to do as a mischief-preventative. That would spoil everything. Aim to interest the boys and girls in the mysterious processes of nature. Encourage them to plan and execute as much of the work as can safely be trusted to them. In a short time you will find that most of them are equal to all the requirements of the ordinary garden. I have often been told by those who have had years of experience in garden-work that at least half one's living for half the year can be obtained from: the garden, even if it happens to be a small one, and my own experience bears out the truth of this statement.
passages.plain: Do not let the child think you give them garden work just to keep them out of trouble. That would ruin everything. Try to interest the boys and girls in the mysterious processes of nature. Encourage them to plan and do as much work as you can safely trust them to do. In a short time, you will find that most of them can handle all the requirements of an ordinary garden. People with years of experience in garden work have told me that you can earn at least half of your living for half of the year from a garden. This is true even if the garden is small. My own experience proves this statement is true.

passages.old: If we grow our own vegetables we are quite sure to have a greater variety to add to the daily bill of fare than would be the case if we were to buy them. We have them when we want them without making a trip to the market for them, or depending on the uncertainties of telephone orders which grocers so frequently fill by sending vegetables of a quan would not satisfy us if we gave them personal inspection before purchasing. The entire family will be delighted with the frequent changes that can be made in the bill of fare, and no one more so than the housewife who often finds it a difficult matter to plan for a variety of food when the family income does not warrant a liberal outlay.
passages.plain: You will have a larger variety of vegetables to eat if you grow them yourself. You will have them when you want them. You will not have to go to the market. You will not have to rely on telephone orders. Grocers often send vegetables in quantities that would not satisfy you if you could inspect them personally. Your entire family will enjoy the frequent changes to your meals. The housewife will be especially happy. She often finds it hard to plan a variety of food when the family income is not large enough for expensive spending.

passages.old: No owner of a bit of ground that can be made into a garden can afford to let it remain unused. If he does so he does it in disregard of the economy which most of us are obliged to consider and practise in these days of high prices and the increasing cost of daily living. Have a garden if you can.
passages.plain: You should not let a piece of land go to waste if you can turn it into a garden. If you leave it unused, you are ignoring the need to save money. Most people must be careful with money today because prices are high and the cost of living is increasing. You should have a garden if you can.

chapters.why: It encourages beginners by explaining that anyone can learn to garden successfully with a little effort and guidance.

chapters.title: Getting the garden ready

passages.old: HE amateur gardener will almost invariably be in too great a hurry to begin gardening operations in the spring. But a few warm days are not sufficient to put the ground in proper condition for seeding, or even for plowing and spading. 'The frost must be allowed to get out of it, and after that an opportunity must be given for surplus water from melting snows and spring rains to drain away before work can be done to any advantage. As a general thing not much can be done in gardening at the North before the first of May.
passages.plain: You will likely be in too much of a hurry to start gardening in the spring. A few warm days are not enough to get the ground ready for seeding, plowing, or spading. You must let the frost leave the ground first. After that, you must let extra water from melting snow and spring rains drain away. Only then can you do work effectively. Generally, you cannot do much gardening in the North before May 1.

passages.old: It is an old saying that ''haste makes waste,' and the gardener who is in too great a hurry often learns the truth which underlies the saying by the failure to germinate of the seed he puts into the ground very early in the season. | Another old saying that should be kept in mind is that ''one swallow does not make a summer." Read '' warm day'"' for ''swallow"' and you will get the force of the statement. It is not advisable to do much at gardening until you are reasonably sure that warm weather has come to stay.
passages.plain: There is an old saying that haste makes waste. A gardener who rushes too much often learns this truth. They see it when seeds fail to grow because they were planted too early in the season. You should also remember another old saying: one swallow does not make a summer. This means one warm day does not mean the season has changed. You should not do much gardening until you are sure that warm weather will stay.

passages.old: Even if earlyplanted seed comes up, spells of cold weather, and often of frost, which we are likely to have at the North until about the first of May, will have such a debilitating effect on comparatively hardy plants that those grown from later sowings, when all conditions are favorable, will come to maturity ahead of them. 'Therefore it will be seen that it is poor policy to be in too great a hurry, and good policy to wait for what the farmer calls "'growing weather" before doing much work in the garden.
passages.plain: Even if you plant seeds early, cold weather and frost can hurt the plants. In the North, these conditions often last until May 1. This damage makes early plants weak. Plants grown later will grow faster and reach maturity sooner because the conditions are better. You should not hurry too much. It is better to wait for growing weather before you do much work in the garden.

passages.old: If very early vegetables are wanted it will be necessary to start them in the hotbed. In another chapter I will give some directions for the making and management of _ this very important adjunct of gardening. The first thing to do in making a garden is to plow or spade it. Plowing is not admissible on small grounds, but where there is room enough to allow a team and plow to operate I would advise it in preference to spading, because it will save a good deal of hard work, and greatly expedite matters.
passages.plain: You must start very early vegetables in a hotbed. I will give directions for making and managing this important gardening tool in another chapter. The first step in making a garden is to plow or spade it. You cannot plow on small grounds. If you have enough room for a team and a plow, I advise you to plow instead of spade. Plowing will save you a lot of hard work and make the process much faster.

passages.old: Before plowing some system of manuring should be decided on, as whatever fertilizer is used should be worked well into the soil, and this the plow can do most effectively. Barn-yard manure, if old and well rotted, is better than anything else I have any knowledge of for all kinds of vegetables, but unfortunately it is seldom obtainable by those who: do not live in the country. There are many commercial fertilizers on the market, but not all kinds of them are adapted to all kinds of soil. In order to secure the best results it is advisable that the amateur gardener should consult some dealer in these fertilizers in his immediate vicinity, or some one who has had personal experience in their use, with a view to making sure that he is getting just the kind best adapted to the soil in his garden.
passages.plain: You should decide on a manuring system before you start plowing. You must work the fertilizer well into the soil. A plow is the best tool for this job. Old and well rotted barn yard manure is the best fertilizer for all kinds of vegetables. However, it is hard to get if you do not live in the country. You can buy many commercial fertilizers. But these fertilizers do not work for every type of soil. To get the best results, you should talk to a local fertilizer dealer. You can also talk to someone who has used them before. This will help you find the best fertilizer for your specific garden soil.

passages.old: It is absolutely necessary that he should do this, in fact, for if he buys at random he runs the risk of getting something that will fail to answer his purpose. While it is always advisable to apply whatever fertilizer is used before plowing, commercial fertilizers can be applied later with good effect; but it will be necessary to apply them in such a manner that they do not come directly into contact with the seed, as many of them are so strong that they kill it. Plow the garden deeply, for by so doing you bring to the surface a stratum of soil in which there is more latent fertility than in that close to the surface.
passages.plain: You must do this. If you buy seeds at random, you might get something that does not work for your needs. It is always best to put fertilizer in the ground before you plow. You can also put commercial fertilizers in later with good results. You must apply them so they do not touch the seed directly. Many of these fertilizers are so strong that they will kill the seed. Plow your garden deeply. This brings up a layer of soil that has more hidden nutrients than the soil near the surface.

passages.old: After plowing, allow the soil to remain as thrown up from the furrow for two or three days. Sunshine and warm air will have a disintegrating effect on it, which will make it easy for you to reduce it under the application of hoe and iron rake to that mellow condition so necessary to the welfare of the plants you propose to grow. It should be worked over and over until not a lump is left in it. You cannot expect to grow good vegetables in a soil that has not been well pulverized before seed is planted.
passages.plain: After you plow the land, let the soil stay in the furrows for two or three days. The sunshine and warm air will break the soil apart. This will make it easier for you to use a hoe and an iron rake to make the soil soft. This soft condition is necessary for the health of the plants you want to grow. You must work the soil over and over until there are no lumps left. You cannot expect to grow good vegetables in soil that is not crushed into small pieces before you plant the seeds.

passages.old: Large grounds, or those of a size that admit of the use-of horses, can be speedily mellowed with the harrow, which should be run over the ground from all directions until it is thoroughly pulverized. In the small garden the rake and hoe will have to take the place of the harrow. Small pieces of ground should be spaded. Let the soil remain as thrown up by the spade for two or three days before attempting to work it. | I have been told by some amateur gardeners that they did not use much manure because trees and shrubs that grew in close proximity to their gardens were so thrifty without manuring that they felt confident that the soil must be quite rich enough for vegetables without resorting to the use of any fertilizer.
passages.plain: You can quickly soften large grounds with a harrow. You should run the harrow over the ground from all directions until the soil is completely broken down. In a small garden, you must use a rake and a hoe instead of a harrow. You should use a spade on small pieces of ground. Let the soil stay as it is after you turn it with the spade for two or three days before you work it again. Some amateur gardeners told me they did not use much manure. They saw that trees and shrubs growing near their gardens grew well without manure. Because of this, they felt sure the soil was rich enough for vegetables without using any fertilizer.

passages.old: 'These persons lacked the experience which would have enabled them to understand the wide difference between tree and vegetable growth. <A tree or a bush sends its roots deeply and widely into the soil, and applies to its uses food that the vegetable cannot send its roots in search of. The roots of most garden plants do not extend far in any direction, nor go very deep; therefore food must be given directly to them if we would secure the best possible result. There are very few gardens in which the natural soil has a sufficient amount of nutriment to produce the effect we aim at without the addition of some kind of plant-food.
passages.plain: These people did not have the experience to understand the big difference between how trees and vegetables grow. A tree or a bush sends its roots deep and wide into the soil. It takes food from places that a vegetable cannot reach. The roots of most garden plants do not go far or very deep. You must give food directly to these roots if you want the best results. There are very few gardens where the natural soil has enough nutrients to produce the results you want without adding some kind of plant food.

passages.old: A rich soil is absolutely necessary in order to hasten development. Unless a vegetable makes a quick growth it is pretty sure to be lacking in tenderness and flavor. Of course it is possible to apply a greater amount than a plant can make use of, thus forcing an unhealthy growth, but this is not likely to happen if we consult the wise old gardener who knows his garden and the plants he grows in it as a mechanic knows the machine he uses,
passages.plain: You need rich soil to make vegetables grow fast. If a vegetable does not grow quickly, it will likely lack flavor and tenderness. You can give a plant more nutrients than it can use. This would force it to grow in an unhealthy way. This is unlikely to happen if you follow the advice of an experienced gardener. A wise gardener knows his garden and his plants just as a mechanic knows his machine.

chapters.why: It teaches the importance of patience and understanding soil conditions before beginning the planting season.

chapters.title: Laying out the garden

passages.old: HERE will be little '"'laying out" to do in the small garden. Here the chief aim will be to make use of every available bit of soil; the beds will be narrow, and the paths between them will be just wide enough to walk in, and these will be the only portions of the ground in which something is not grown. Not much chance for planning, you see. In the larger garden it will be not only possible, but advisable, to do considerable planning. If a garden-cultivator is used, and this should be done whenever possible, plan for rows that will enable you to run it the entire length of the garden without turning.
passages.plain: You will not have much layout work to do in a small garden. Your main goal is to use every bit of soil. The garden beds will be narrow. The paths between them will be just wide enough for you to walk on. These paths are the only parts of the ground where you will not grow anything. You do not have much room for planning in a small garden. In a larger garden, you can and should plan more. If you use a garden cultivator, you should do so whenever possible. Plan your rows so that you can run the cultivator the entire length of the garden without turning.

passages.old: Beds are no longer in favor with gardeners who aim to reduce the work to be done to the minimum, for in them the cultivator cannot be used to advantage, and weeding cannot be done with the facility which characterizes row-planting, nor can the hoe be used as effectively. There is really no argument that can be advanced in favor of the old bedding system for gardens in which we propose to use labor-saving implements. If possible, have the rows run north and south. This enables the sun to get at the eround lengthwise of the rows, and between them, which it could not do if they ran east and west, as the plants in them would shade all the ground except that in the first and most southerly row.
passages.plain: Gardeners who want to do as little work as possible do not use garden beds anymore. You cannot use a cultivator well in beds. You also cannot weed as easily as you can with row planting. You cannot use a hoe as effectively in beds either. There is no reason to use the old bedding system if you want to use tools that save labor. If you can, make your rows run north and south. This lets the sun reach the ground along the rows and between them. The sun cannot do this if the rows run east and west. In that case, the plants would shade all the ground except for the first and most southern row.

passages.old: It is not enough that the sun should get at the tops of the plants. _ The soil needs its vivifying effect. | Plant with regard to the height and habit of the vegetables you propose to grow. Give corn a place at the side of the garden. 'Then peas which grow tall enough to require bushing, and then beans, working down through potatoes, tomatoes, and beets and other lowgrowing kinds to. onions, radishes, and cucumbers. If the garden-cultivator is to be used, leave a space about eighteen inches wide between the rows to work in.
passages.plain: The sun must reach more than just the tops of your plants. The soil also needs the sun's life-giving effect. You should plant your vegetables based on how tall they grow and their shape. Put corn at the side of the garden. Next, plant peas that grow tall enough to need staking. Then plant beans. Work your way down to potatoes, tomatoes, beets, and other low-growing plants. Finish with onions, radishes, and cucumbers. If you plan to use a garden cultivator, leave a space about eighteen inches wide between the rows so you can work in them.

passages.old: This implement can be adjusted to fit any width desired. Its teeth can be set to throw the soil toward a plant or away from it. It can be LAYING OUT THE GARDEN | made to do deep or shallow work, as the case may require. As a general thing, after a plant has attained some size we throw the soil toward it. If the teeth are set to do this we go down one side of the row and back on the other, thus throwing the soil about the plant alike on both sides.
passages.plain: You can adjust this tool to fit any width you want. You can set the teeth to throw soil toward a plant or away from it. You can also make it do deep or shallow work depending on what you need. Generally, you should throw the soil toward a plant once it reaches a certain size. If the teeth are set to do this, you should walk down one side of the row and then back on the other side. This will throw soil around the plant on both sides.

passages.old: It will probably be necessary to remove some weeds in the row, which cannot be reached by the cultivator. This can be done most effectively by the use of a hoe which is triangular in shape, with the handle-socket in the center of it. One side is a blade like the ordinary hoe. 'The other comes to a sharp point, with which it is possible to work close to a plant without running any risk of injuring it, something that cannot be done with the ordinary wide-bladed hoe. Weeds that grow up side by side with vegetable seedlings can be picked away from them so easily, and without disturbing them in the least, that no hand-pulling will have to be resorted to in cleaning the rows.
passages.plain: You will probably need to remove some weeds in the row. You cannot reach these weeds with a cultivator. You can do this best by using a triangular hoe. The handle socket is in the center of this hoe. One side of the hoe looks like a normal hoe blade. The other side comes to a sharp point. You can use this sharp point to work close to a plant. You will not risk hurting the plant with this tool. You cannot do this with a normal wide-bladed hoe. You can pick away weeds that grow next to vegetable seedlings. You can do this easily without moving the seedlings at all. You will not have to pull the weeds by hand to clean the rows.

passages.old: Where the garden-cultivator is used there will be very little work to do with the hoe, as this implement stirs the soil and uproots weeds at the same time. But in the small garden either hoe or weeding-hook will come into daily use. The weeding-hook is a most important tool, though its cost is but ten or fifteen cents. It enables one to do a good deal of weeding in a short time, does its work well, and does away entirely with handpulling, which has heretofore been one of the chief arguments that men have advanced against gardening.
passages.plain: You will have very little work to do with a hoe if you use a garden cultivator. This tool stirs the soil and pulls up weeds at the same time. In a small garden, you will use either a hoe or a weeding hook every day. The weeding hook is a very important tool. It only costs ten or fifteen cents. It lets you pull many weeds in a short time. It works well and removes the need for pulling weeds by hand. Pulling weeds by hand was one of the main reasons people used to argue against gardening.

chapters.why: The principles of maximizing space and orienting rows for sunlight remain fundamental to efficient modern gardening.

chapters.title: Planting the garden

passages.old: OST persons make the serious mistake of covering garden seed too deeply. Very small seed needs hardly any covering. Indeed, it does its best, as a general thing, when simply scattered on the surface and pressed down into the soil by a smooth board. This embeds the seed in the soil, which is made firm enough under the pressure of the board to retain a sufficient amount of moisture to assist germination. Very fine seed often fails to sprout if covered too deeply. But most of the seed of garden vegetables is not fine enough to admit of this method of planting.
passages.plain: Many people make the mistake of covering garden seeds too deeply. Very small seeds need almost no covering. These seeds do best when you scatter them on the surface. You should then press them into the soil with a smooth board. This puts the seed into the soil. The pressure of the board makes the soil firm. This firm soil holds enough moisture to help the seeds grow. Very fine seeds often fail to sprout if you cover them too deeply. However, most vegetable seeds are not fine enough to use this specific planting method.

passages.old: If a seed-sower is not used, little furrows should be made by drawing a stick through the soil, into which the seed should be dropped as evenly as possible. It should then be covered lightly and the soil should be pressed down with the hoe to make it comparatively firm. The probabilities are that many more plants will come up than it is advisable to let grow. 'These surplus seedlings should be removed from the rows as soon as the plants get a good start. Nearly all gardeners make use of the seedsower.
passages.plain: If you do not use a seed-sower, you should make small furrows. You can do this by pulling a stick through the soil. Drop the seeds into these furrows as evenly as possible. Cover the seeds lightly. Press the soil down with a hoe to make it firm. Many more plants will likely grow than you want to keep. You should remove these extra seedlings from the rows as soon as the plants start to grow well. Almost all gardeners use a seed-sower.

passages.old: This is an implement that can be adjusted to sow all kinds of seed more evenly than it can be sown by hand, and it can be sown thickly or thinly, as desired, and at any required depth. It cannot be used to much advantage in the very small garden, where only a small quantity of each kind of seed will be made use of, but in large gardens it will be found as much a labor-saver as the garden-cultivator. It is always advisable to plant for a succession if the garden is large enough to admit of it.
passages.plain: This tool can be adjusted to plant all kinds of seeds more evenly than you can do by hand. You can plant the seeds thickly or thinly. You can also plant them at any depth you want. This tool is not very useful in a very small garden. That is because you would only use a small amount of each seed. However, in large gardens, this tool saves as much labor as a garden cultivator. You should always plant in a succession if your garden is large enough for it.

passages.old: By planting at intervals of ten days or two weeks it is possible to have fresh vegetables throughout almost the entire season. Where this is done it will not be advisable to plant very much of any one kind. Among almost all vegetables there are early, medium, and late varieties. Some of - each of these should be planted in all gardens of a size to warrant so doing. In the small garden I would advise the choice of the later varieties, as these are almost without exception superior in flavor to the earlier kinds, which are grown more on account of earliness than quality.
passages.plain: You can have fresh vegetables almost all season by planting them every ten days or two weeks. If you do this, you should not plant too much of any one kind. Most vegetables have early, medium, and late varieties. You should plant some of each variety in any garden large enough to do so. For a small garden, I suggest choosing the later varieties. These varieties almost always taste better than the early kinds. Early kinds are usually grown for their timing rather than their quality.

chapters.why: The text provides fundamental principles of seed depth and spacing that remain essential for successful germination today.

chapters.title: Seeds that give best results

passages.old: T is very important that seed of only the best kind should be used, if we would grow vegetables of superior quality. Every gardener of experience will indorse the truth of this statement. Said one amateur gardener to me when I gave him this advice: ''Why should one be so particular about the seed? It's the culture that you give the plant that counts. Plant any kind of seed that happens to be handiest and take good care of the plants that grow from it and you'll have good vegetables."' To some extent what he said was true, but he had yet to learn that there is a vast difference between ordinary seed and seed that has bred into it by careful culture the superior qualities which characterize the choicest varieties of all our garden plants.
passages.plain: You must use only the best kind of seeds if you want to grow high quality vegetables. Every experienced gardener agrees with this. One amateur gardener told me that I was wrong when I gave him this advice. He asked why someone should be so careful about seeds. He said that the way you care for the plant is what matters most. He claimed you can plant any seed that is nearby and take good care of the plants to get good vegetables. He was partly right. However, he did not know that there is a big difference between ordinary seeds and seeds that have been bred for superior qualities. These special seeds have the best traits of the finest garden plants.

passages.old: There is such a thing as aristocracy of seed, and no seed that is lacking in this feature can be expected to afford the satisfaction that results from the use of the best. No amount of culture can make a superior vegetable from plants grown from inferior seed. Bear this in mind, and buy only the best seed on the market, be your garden large or small. The smaller it is, the greater the importance of using only the best. "But how are we who know very little about such things to know which 7s the best?"' some one may ask.
passages.plain: There is a difference between high-quality seeds and low-quality seeds. You cannot expect to get great results from poor seeds. No amount of careful gardening can turn a bad seed into a superior vegetable. You must remember this. Buy only the best seeds available on the market. This applies whether your garden is large or small. If your garden is small, it is even more important to use the best seeds. Someone might ask, how can you know which seed is the best if you do not know much about gardening?

passages.old: The only answer I can make to this question is this: We have in this country many seed firms that have been in existence for years, some of them over half a century, and these have built up for themselves a reputation for handling only seed of the very best. varieties of garden vegetables that it is possible to grow. Inferior sorts have been discarded from time to time as those of superior merit have been produced. 'These firms, proud and jealous of the reputation they have gained, cannot afford to deal in anything that is not up to their standard of ''the best.'?'
passages.plain: I can only answer the question this way. Our country has many seed companies. Some of these companies have existed for over fifty years. They have built a reputation for selling only the best types of garden vegetables. They remove lower quality types as better ones are created. These companies are proud of their reputations. They cannot sell anything that does not meet their high standards for the best.

passages.old: From these dealers you can _ be sure of getting seed that can always be depended on to give the highest degree of satisfaction. The seed they sell you may cost a: little more than some of the newer dealers ask for theirs, but the certainty of getting what you want makes it well worth while to invest some extra money in it. Cheap seed, that which is advertised as being ''just as good as higher-priced seed for a much smaller amount of money'', is likely to prove as cheap in quality as in price.
passages.plain: You can be sure to get reliable seeds from these dealers. These seeds will always give you the best results. The seeds they sell might cost a little more than newer dealers charge. However, the certainty of getting what you want makes it worth spending the extra money. Cheap seed is often advertised as being just as good as expensive seed for less money. This cheap seed will likely be low in quality as well as price.

chapters.why: Choosing high-quality seeds remains the fundamental first step for ensuring a successful and productive vegetable garden.

chapters.title: Early garden work

passages.old: FTER planting the garden there will be a little interval of leisure while the seed that has been put into the ground is germinating. | Then will come the time of early warfare with the weeds. Here is where the weedinghook of which I have spoken will come into play in the small garden. 'This little implement is in the form of a claw, with five or six fingers, each about an inch long, and shaped so that they reach into the ground and take a firm hold of whatever plants they are placed over.
passages.plain: After you plant the garden, you will have some free time. This is because the seeds in the ground are starting to grow. Then it will be time to fight the weeds. You will use the weedinghook in your small garden. This tool looks like a claw. It has five or six fingers. Each finger is about one inch long. The fingers are shaped to go into the ground. They grab onto any plants you put them over.

passages.old: It can be so operated that these fingers, working close to plants which it is not desired to uproot, will tear away the weeds without disturbing the other plants, and the soil will be left in ight and mellow condition, as if a tiny rake had been drawn through it. With this tool the work can be done with great rapidity. No owner of a garden, large or small, can afford to be without it. It should be used to supplement the work of the cultivator, which can be depended upon to take care of all the weeds between the rows, but which cannot be worked among the plants an the row. | Weeding should be begun as soon as the plants are of a size that makes it possible to tell which is seedling and which is weed.
passages.plain: You can use this tool to pull weeds near your plants without pulling up the plants themselves. The soil will stay loose and soft. It will look like a tiny rake went through it. You can work very fast with this tool. Every gardener needs one regardless of the size of their garden. Use this tool to help the cultivator. The cultivator handles weeds between the rows. However, the cultivator cannot work among the plants in the rows. You should start weeding as soon as the plants are big enough to tell the difference between a seedling and a weed.

passages.old: By beginning the work of clearing the garden at this period, and doing it thoroughly, and continuing it at intervals thereafter, it will be a comparatively easy matter to keep weeds under control. But if they are allowed to get a strong start, as they will in an incredibly short time if let alone, it will be a difficult matter to subdue them and keep the upper hand during the rest of the season. It is very important that they should be given to understand, at the outset, that they will not be tolerated in your garden.
passages.plain: Start clearing your garden now. Do the work thoroughly. Continue to do it at intervals later. This will make it easier to control weeds. If you let weeds grow for a very short time, they will get a strong start. It will then be hard to stop them or control them for the rest of the season. You must make it clear from the beginning that you will not tolerate weeds in your garden.

passages.old: This will necessitate early work and careful and regular attention thereafter, but it will not be the laborious work that so many persons think it is if it is begun at the right season and always carried on on the offensive. It is when weeds have been allowed to intrench themselves firmly in the garden that this work becomes disagreeable. Nor is it work that will require a good deal of one's time. In the cultivation of a garden it is the little attentions, given when needed, that count, rather than the amount of labor and time expended there, as you will find when you come to have a garden of your own.
passages.plain: You will need to start early and give the garden careful and regular attention. It will not be as hard as many people think if you start at the right time and stay ahead of the weeds. The work becomes unpleasant only when weeds have a chance to grow deep into the ground. This task will not take up a lot of your time. In gardening, the small actions you take when they are needed are what matter most. You will see this when you have your own garden. It is not about the total amount of labor or time you spend.

passages.old: If there are any vacant places in the beds or rows, fill with plants~taken from places where they stand too thick. In the small garden there should be not one vacant spot. Every bit of soil should be made to do its share of work in the production of some vegetable. If weeds are kept down during the early part of the season there ought not to be many during the latter part of it. But there will be no time when there will not be some to wage warfare against, and every gardener should make it a rule to destroy every one that gets a start as soon as discovered, for, by preventing it from developing seed, we can save ourselves a good deal of work next season.
passages.plain: Fill any empty spaces in the beds or rows with plants. Take these plants from places where they grow too close together. Your small garden should have no empty spots. Every bit of soil must help produce a vegetable. If you keep weeds down early in the season, there should not be many weeds later in the season. However, there will always be some weeds to fight. Every gardener should make it a rule to destroy every weed as soon as you find it. By stopping a weed from making seeds, you can save yourself a lot of work next season.

passages.old: One weed will bear seed enough to fill the whole garden with its progeny if - allowed to do so. | If the soil was properly fertilized at planting-time it will not be necessary to apply more fertilizer, if any, until the latter part of the season, and then only a small amount will be required, just enough to enable the soil to do its share in ripening off the plants that are growing in it. But if, at any time, the plants seem to lag or come to a standstill enough should be given to stimulate active growth.
passages.plain: One weed can produce enough seeds to fill your entire garden with its offspring if you let it. If you fertilized the soil correctly when you planted, you do not need to add more fertilizer until late in the season. At that time, you only need a small amount. This amount should just be enough to help the soil ripen the plants growing in it. However, if your plants seem to stop growing or slow down at any time, you should give them enough fertilizer to start active growth again.

passages.old: Careful watch should be kept of everything in the garden, and prompt advantage should be taken of any tendency toward slow development by making fresh applications of whatever fertilizer was used at the beginning of the season. In order to attain the success that the gardener aims at in the cultivation of vegetables it is absolutely necessary to keep them going steadily ahead from start to finish, and this can only be done by supplying them with a generous amount of plant-food. There should be no alternations of liberal feeding and lack of feeding.
passages.plain: You must watch everything in the garden carefully. If you see any plants growing slowly, you should act quickly. You must add more of the same fertilizer you used at the start of the season. To be successful in growing vegetables, you must keep the plants growing steadily from start to finish. You can only do this by giving them a large amount of plant food. You should not switch between giving them a lot of food and giving them no food.

chapters.why: The text provides practical advice on using specific tools and early intervention to manage weeds effectively.

chapters.title: Vegetable plants in the house

passages.old: ANY persons would like to grow early vegetables. With a view to "getting the start of the season"' and, incidentally, of their neighbors, they sow seed in pots and boxes in March and April and attempt to get an ''early start" for plants that will form a basis of supply for family use while they are waiting for the development of the general crop from seed sown in the garden after the weather has become sufficiently warm to warrant outdoor gardening. In some instances comparative success has resulted from plants started into growth in the house, but nine times out of ten, it is safe to say, the result has been entire failure.
passages.plain: Many people want to grow vegetables early. They want to start the season before their neighbors do. They sow seeds in pots and boxes during March and April. They try to get an early start on plants for their family to eat. They do this while they wait for the main crop to grow. They sow the main crop in the garden once the weather is warm enough for outdoor gardening. Sometimes people have some success growing plants inside the house. However, nine times out of ten, these plants fail completely.

passages.old: The seedlings grow fairly well at first, but soon become weak and die. If, by chance,.a few survive until conditions warrant putting them in the ground, they are so lacking in vitality that the change from indoors to outdoors is pretty sure to be the end of them. I would never advise trying to grow plants from seed, in the house, unless the grower understands beforehand the drawbacks to plant-growth which prevail in the average dwelling, and is willing to do all he can to overcome them. Simply filling boxes or pots with earth, putting seed into them, and supplying water will not insure success.
passages.plain: The seedlings grow well at first. Soon they become weak and die. If a few survive until it is time to put them in the ground, they lack enough strength to survive the move. Moving them from indoors to outdoors will likely kill them. I would not advise growing plants from seed in a house unless you understand the problems that happen to plants in a normal home. You must be willing to do everything you can to fix those problems. Simply filling boxes or pots with dirt and putting seeds in them with water will not make them grow successfully.

passages.old: One of the unfavorable conditions which seedling plants must struggle against is too much heat, if they are kept in the livingroom. An undue amount of warmth forces them into abnormal development in the early stages of their growth, and a little later on there comes a reaction from the weakness thus brought about, and this reaction is almost invariably death to the tender plant. Another unfavorable condition is the result of indiscriminate watering. The soil is either kept too wet or too dry. To grow good plants there must be an even supply of moisture. | A third unfortunate condition is the result of failure to give the plants a liberal supply of fresh air.
passages.plain: Seedlings face several bad conditions. Too much heat in a living room is one problem. Excessive warmth causes abnormal growth in the early stages. Later, the plant reacts to this weakness. This reaction usually kills the tender plant. Another bad condition is irregular watering. This happens when the soil is too wet or too dry. You must provide an even supply of moisture to grow good plants. A third bad condition is a lack of fresh air. You must give the plants a liberal supply of fresh air.

passages.old: It is possible, now eves to overcome these conditions and grow really good plants from seed in the living-room, but it cannot be done unless the amateur gardener is suffciently interested in the undertaking to give his plants all the attention they need. Instead of keeping them in the livingroom, which in most instances will have a temperature of 79 or 80°, I would advise giving them place in a room opening off the sitting-room, where the temperature can be so regulated that it will not go above 65° at any time.
passages.plain: You can overcome these conditions and grow very good plants from seeds in your living room. However, you can only do this if you are interested enough to give your plants all the attention they need. I advise against keeping them in the living room. Most living rooms have a temperature of 79 or 80 degrees. Instead, put your plants in a room that opens off the sitting room. You can regulate the temperature in that room so it never goes above 65 degrees.

passages.old: There is far less danger of plants suffering from a low temperature than of their being injured by an excess of heat. If the room in which they are kept has snug windows, in most instances it will get all the warmth that is needed by leaving open at night the door which connects it with the living-room. If the weather is very cold, the plants can be removed, temporarily, to the living-room, or they can be covered with newspapers. Thick paper shades at the windows will do much to keep out cold and prevent draughts.
passages.plain: Plants are in more danger from too much heat than from low temperatures. Most of the time, your room will stay warm enough if you have tight windows. You can leave the door to the living room open at night to let in warmth. If the weather gets very cold, you can move the plants to the living room for a short time. You can also cover the plants with newspapers. Putting thick paper shades on the windows will help block out the cold and stop drafts.

passages.old: Stormsash will do this most effectively, but it interferes with giving the young plants the fresh air they need. Therefore I would prefer the shades, and depend upon removal! to a warmer place on extra-cold nights. Fresh air will be found a most important factor in the growth of seedling plants indoors. Unless it can be given it will be almost impossible to grow any plant well in the ordinary dwelling. It should be admitted to the room on every pleasant day by opening a window at the top, or a door at some distance from the plants.
passages.plain: A storm sash works best for this, but it stops young plants from getting the fresh air they need. I prefer using shades instead. You should move the plants to a warmer place on extra cold nights. Fresh air is very important for growing seedlings indoors. It is almost impossible to grow plants well in a normal house without fresh air. You should let air into the room on every pleasant day. You can do this by opening a window at the top or a door far away from the plants.

passages.old: The fresh, cold air should be allowed to mix with the warm air in the room before it comes in contact with the plants, as a chill will often do about as much damage as a touch of frost. Watering these plants is a matter of prime importance. Generally water is applied carelessly and irregularly, too much _ to-day, and none at all to-morrow. We saturate the soil with it while only enough is required to make it moist. An over-supply of water at the roots, combined with too much heat and lack of fresh air, will undermine the constitution of any plant, because such a combination excites unnatural development, and this means a lowering of the vital force to the danger-point.
passages.plain: You should let the fresh cold air mix with the warm air in the room before it touches the plants. A chill can damage plants as much as frost does. Watering these plants is very important. People usually water them carelessly and irregularly. They might give too much water today and none tomorrow. You should not soak the soil. You only need enough water to make the soil moist. Too much water at the roots combined with too much heat and a lack of fresh air will hurt the plant. This combination causes unnatural growth. This lowers the plant's vital force to a dangerous point.

passages.old: I have devised a method by which I have succeeded in controlling the supply of moisture in the soil to my complete satisfaction. I use boxes about four inches deep to start my plants in, In the bottom of these boxes I put sphagnum moss. There should be at least an inch of it after it has been pressed down by the weight of the soil above. The bottom of the seed-box is bored full of small holes. Each box sets in a shallow pan of galvanized iron, on a layer of coarse gravel, which raises it enough to allow water to circulate freely under it.
passages.plain: I created a method to control the moisture in the soil. I use boxes that are about four inches deep to start my plants. I put sphagnum moss at the bottom of these boxes. You should have at least one inch of moss left after you press the soil down on top of it. You must drill many small holes in the bottom of the seed box. Each box sits in a shallow pan made of galvanized iron. The pan has a layer of coarse gravel. This setup raises the box so that water can move freely under it.

passages.old: Water is poured into the iron pan, using enough to come up about half an inch above the bottom of the seedbox, or in contact with the moss in it, and it should be kept at this height at all times. The moss absorbs the moisture like a sponge, and the soil above constantly sucks up all that is needed to keep it in a sufficiently moist condition to meet the requirements of the plants growing in it. The absorbent qualities of the moss are such that an excessive amount of moisture is never communicated to the soil above.
passages.plain: Pour water into the iron pan. Use enough water to reach about half an inch above the bottom of the seedbox. The water must touch the moss inside the box. You must keep the water at this height at all times. The moss acts like a sponge and soaks up the water. The soil above the moss pulls up the moisture it needs to stay wet for the plants. The moss is very absorbent. It prevents too much water from reaching the soil above.

passages.old: Thus I secure a steady and even supply, which does away entirely with the danger resulting from the application of water to the surface of the soil from watering-pot or basin. If the temperature can be controlled in such a way that it will not vary much from 60 to 65°, if the soil can be kept moist but never wet, and fresh air can be given in generous quantity cae, it will be found a comparatively easy matter to grow plants satisfactorily from seed in the house, and have them in such healthy condition by the time it is safe to put them out in the garden that they will average up well with the plants the professional gardener raises in. hotbed and eold-frame. By the use of such plants, and such plants only, can we expect to grow early vegetables successfully.
passages.plain: This method gives you a steady and even supply of water. It removes the danger of watering the surface of the soil with a pot or basin. You can grow plants from seeds in your house easily if you follow these rules. You must keep the temperature between 60 and 65 degrees. You must keep the soil moist but never wet. You must give the plants a large amount of fresh air. You will have healthy plants by the time it is safe to move them to the garden. These plants will be as good as the ones a professional gardener grows in a hotbed or cold-frame. You can only grow early vegetables successfully by using these types of plants.

chapters.why: It explains the fundamental environmental requirements for indoor seedling growth that remain relevant for modern home gardeners.

chapters.title: Standard varieties of vegetables

passages.old: 'HE amateur gardener will find it extremely perplexing work to make a satisfactory selection of varieties of vegetables to grow in his garden. He knows quite well, as a general thing, what kinds he wants to grow, but when he comes to a consultation of the seedsmen's catalogues he discovers that of each kind of vegetable listed therein there are so many varieties mentioned that he is bewildered. Most of them are described as being so desirable that he cannot help getting the impression that if he rules out this or that one he is likely to deprive himself of the very thing from which he would obtain the highest degree of satisfaction.
passages.plain: You will find it very confusing to choose which types of vegetables to grow in your garden. You know generally what kinds you want to grow. However, when you look at the seed catalogs, you will see so many varieties for each vegetable that you will feel overwhelmed. Most of them are described as being very good. You might feel like you will miss out on the best option if you do not choose a specific one.

passages.old: Nine times out of ten he finds, after going through the catalogues and marking the kinds and varieties that appeal to him most forcibly, that he has a list which would furnish enough seed to supply an average-sized market-garden. I would advise the amateur gardener to attempt the culture of only a few of the many varieties described in the catalogues, and these of the very best. But what constitutes ''the very best"' is a hard matter for him to decide where all are described by adjectives in the superlative degree.
passages.plain: Most of the time, a person finds that their list of favorite seeds is enough to supply a medium-sized market garden. I advise the amateur gardener to try growing only a few of the varieties listed in the catalogs. You should choose the very best ones. However, it is hard for you to decide which ones are the best because the catalogs describe all of them as being the best.

passages.old: He will find, by comparing the catalogues of the various seed firms, that there are described in most of them certain varieties of each kind of vegetable that seem common to all, along with many other varieties whose names differ greatly, though the descriptions of them indicate that there is not much difference in quality, or in other general respects. If he confines his selection to such varieties of each kind as the various dealers list under the same names in their catalogues he will be making no mistake, for the fact that all . leading dealers carry these varieties in stock is sufficient proof that they are standard varieties, and of such superior merit that no up-to-date dealer can afford to exclude them from his list. | Take, for instance, Stowell's Evergreen sweet-corn, and Champion of England pea.
passages.plain: You can compare the catalogs of different seed companies. You will see that most of them list certain types of vegetables that appear in every catalog. They also list many other types with different names. However, the descriptions show that these different names do not mean the vegetables are very different in quality. You will not make a mistake if you only choose the varieties that every dealer lists under the same names. The fact that all leading dealers keep these varieties in stock proves they are standard types. These varieties have such high quality that a modern dealer cannot afford to leave them out of their list. For example, you can look at Stowell's Evergreen sweet-corn and Champion of England pea.

passages.old: All dealers handle these, because they are standard, and always in demand because their superior qualities have made them. universal favorites wherever grown. ' But they have other varieties of the same vegetable of which each makes a specialty, under names which will be found in no catalogue but their own. Many of these are doubtless possessors of all the good qualities claimed for them, but this we cannot be sure about. But the sorts which are common to all are those of whose merit there can be no two opinions.
passages.plain: All dealers sell these vegetables. They are standard items that people always want to buy. Their high quality has made them favorites everywhere. However, dealers also have other varieties of the same vegetable. Each dealer specializes in different types. You will only find these special names in their own catalogs. Many of these varieties might have all the good qualities they claim to have. We cannot be sure about that. The common varieties are the ones that everyone agrees are good.

passages.old: 'These are the varieties the inexperienced gardener can select with the assurance that he is getting the best thing of its kind on the market. In this chapter I propose to make mention of only such kinds of vegetables as I have grown in my own garden. I do this because so many beginners in gardening prefer to depend on the advice of some one who has familiarized himself with the merits of the various vegetables adapted to ordinary gardening. And I propose to give with each such brief cultural directions as seem of most importance, thus making it possible for the amateur to avoid some of the mistakes that might be made if he were wholly ignorant of the requirements of his plants. .
passages.plain: You can choose these varieties because they are the best of their kind on the market. In this chapter, I will only talk about vegetables that I have grown in my own garden. I do this because many beginners prefer to follow the advice of someone who knows the benefits of different vegetables for regular gardens. I will give brief instructions for each vegetable that seem most important. This will help you avoid mistakes that happen when you do not know what your plants need.

passages.old: After having experimented with many kinds I have pinned my faith to the kinds I shall make mention of, and I have no hesitancy in recommending them to the attention of all gardeners, feeling confident that a trial of them will bear me out in the statement that no better list can be made. There may be others of equal or superior merit, but if there are I have still to find out what they are. Asparagus ~ Taking the list alphabetically, the first vegetable to consider is asparagus. Conover's Colossal seems to combine all the merits of the several varieties on the market in such a degree as to give it a place at the head of the list of desirable kinds for ordinary garden culture.
passages.plain: I have tried many different kinds of vegetables. I now trust the specific types I am about to mention. I recommend them to all gardeners. I am confident that if you try them, you will see that no better list can be made. There might be other types that are just as good or better. If they exist, I still need to find out what they are. Asparagus. I am listing the vegetables in alphabetical order. The first vegetable to consider is asparagus. Conover's Colossal seems to have all the best qualities of the different varieties sold on the market. It deserves a place at the top of the list of good types for a normal garden.

passages.old: It is tender, fine-flavored, and very productive. A dozen plants, after becoming well established, will furnish all that will be required by a family of four or five persons. , _ In order to secure good crops of this delicious vegetable it will be necessary to dig up the soil in which it is to be planted to the depth of two or three feet, and fill the bottom of the excavation with strong manure. Pack this down firmly, and then return to the trench the soil thrown out from it, fertilizing this well as you do so.
passages.plain: This vegetable is tender and has a good flavor. It produces a lot of food. Twelve plants will provide enough for a family of four or five people once they are established. To get a good crop, you must dig the soil to a depth of two or three feet. Fill the bottom of the hole with strong manure. Pack the manure down firmly. Put the soil back into the trench. Mix the soil with fertilizer well as you put it back.

passages.old: While asparagus will grow in a soil that is not at all rich, and will live on indefinitely under all kinds of neglect and abuse, it must be given plenty of strong food and good care in order to enable it to do itself justice. I would not advise attempting to grow it from seed, as it takes a long time for seedling plants to reach maturity. JI would get two- or three-yearold plants. Set them about eighteen inches apart and at least four inches below the surface. Keep weeds and grass away from them.
passages.plain: Asparagus can grow in poor soil. It can live for a long time even if you neglect it or treat it badly. However, you must give it plenty of strong food and good care so it can grow well. I do not suggest trying to grow it from seed. It takes a long time for seedlings to reach maturity. You should get plants that are two or three years old. Place them about eighteen inches apart. Put them at least four inches below the surface. Keep weeds and grass away from them.

passages.old: Give the asparagus-bed a place in the garden by itself, preferably along a fence or in some location where it will not interfere with other plants which call for the frequent use of the garden-cultivator. On no account plant it in that part of the garden where it will be necessary to use a plow, for it is a plant that must be left undisturbed if you would have it do its best. Cover the beds with coarse manure in the fall, and work this into the soil about, the plants in spring.
passages.plain: Give the asparagus bed its own space in the garden. Put it along a fence or in a spot where it will not get in the way of other plants. You should not have to use a garden cultivator on these plants. Do not plant them in a part of the garden where you need to use a plow. You must leave the plants undisturbed so they can grow well. Cover the beds with coarse manure in the fall. Work this manure into the soil in the spring.

passages.old: Beans Mammoth Stringless Green Pod matures early, and is very tender, fine-flavored, and productive. It is a general favorite for the home garden. Golden Wax is later than the green-podded variety mentioned above. It is valuable as a string-bean, and for shelling. Beans are quite tender, therefore they should not be planted until the weather becomes warm and settled. Plant in rows two feet apart, and about four inches apart in the row, or in hills of three or four plants each. Cultivate frequently during the early part of summer, throwing the soil toward the plants.
passages.plain: Mammoth Stringless Green Pod beans mature early. They are tender and have a good flavor. They produce a lot of beans. They are a popular choice for home gardens. Golden Wax beans mature later than the green pod variety. They are good for eating as string beans and for shelling. Beans are very tender. You should not plant them until the weather is warm and steady. Plant them in rows. Space the rows two feet apart. Space the plants about four inches apart in each row. You can also plant them in hills with three or four plants in each hill. Work the soil often during the early summer. Throw the soil toward the plants.

passages.old: Do not work among them while they are wet from dew or rain. If a pole-bean is wanted, Improved Lima will be found extremely satisfactory because of its productiveness and its fine, buttery flavor. This class supplies the table with shelled beans only, its pods being too tough to use as a string-bean. Plant in hills of six or eight, setting a pole six or seven feet tall in the center of each hill for the plants to climb by. | Beet I would advise two varieties of this vegetable where the garden is large enough to warrant the use of more than one.
passages.plain: Do not work in the garden while the plants are wet from rain or dew. If you want a pole bean, the Improved Lima variety is very good. It produces a lot of beans and has a fine, buttery flavor. This type of bean is only good for eating once the shells are removed. The pods are too tough to eat like string beans. Plant them in rows of six or eight. Put a pole that is six or seven feet tall in the center of each row so the plants can climb it. For beets, I suggest growing two different varieties if your garden is large enough to have more than one.

passages.old: Crosby's Egyptian stands at the head of the list as an early variety. It is remarkably tender, and has a sugary flavor that is most delicious. passages.plain: Crosby's Egyptian is an early variety. It is very tender and has a delicious sugary flavor. I recommend Crimson Globe as a second variety. It is very sweet and has a fine flavor. It reaches perfection during the late summer. It keeps well. You should store a large amount of it in the cellar for the winter. Plant the seeds in rows sixteen to eighteen inches apart. Plant them thickly. Use the extra plants as greens while they are young and tender. You can use both the tops and the roots.

passages.old: 'The trench should be about two feet deep. Spread straw in the bottom of it, and place the cabbage on it, head down, with the large leaves folded well together. Then cover with three or four inches of hay, and bank up with soil. Put a board over this to shed rain. The cabbage will freeze, but if left in the ground until the frost is gradually extracted from it it will be found crisp and brittle, and much more satisfactory for table use than that which is wintered in the cellar.
passages.plain: Dig a trench about two feet deep. Put straw on the bottom of the trench. Place the cabbage on the straw. Put the cabbage head down. Fold the large leaves together well. Cover the cabbage with three or four inches of hay. Bank up the hay with soil. Put a board over the soil to keep off the rain. The cabbage will freeze. Leave it in the ground until the frost slowly leaves it. The cabbage will be crisp and brittle. It will be much better for eating than cabbage kept in a cellar during winter.

passages.old: Care must be taken to exclude rain. If water gets to it it will be ruined. It is a good plan to cover the trench with oilcloth or tarred paper, both being waterproof. Cauliflower This is a favorite vegetable when well grown and properly cared for. It requires a rich soil, a location well exposed to the sun, and frequent applications of water if the season happens to be a dry one. Cultivate as you would cabbage. passages.plain: You must be careful to keep rain away. The plant will be ruined if water touches it. You should cover the trench with oilcloth or tarred paper because both are waterproof. Cauliflower is a popular vegetable when it is grown well and cared for properly. It needs rich soil and a place with plenty of sun. You must give it water often if the season is dry. You should grow it the same way you grow cabbage. To have them early, you should start the plants in the hotbed. Move them to the cold frame as soon as they have three leaves.

passages.old: Put into the open ground as soon as the soil is in good working condition. Set the plants about two feet apart. passages.plain: Put the plants into the open ground as soon as the soil is ready for work. Place the plants about two feet apart. When the heads have formed, you should bleach them. passages.old: It is rich and sweet in flavor. Red Intermediate is a later variety, excellent for fall and winter use. passages.plain: This vegetable has a rich and sweet flavor. Red Intermediate is a later variety. It is excellent for use in the fall and winter. Not many people put this plant in their gardens.
