After that, it becomes a standard vegetable on the housewife's list of must-haves. It adds a delightful flavor to vegetable soups.

passages.old: Celery The seed of early celery should be sown in the hotbed. 'Transplant the seedlings to the cold-frame and allow them to remain there until May. Then set in the richest soil at your disposal, six inches apart in the row. Blanch by setting up boards a foot or more in width each side the row, allowing an opening about three inches wide at the. top through which the plants can get a little light. For late and winter. use, sow the seeds in open ground in May. Bleach by earthing up gradually, as the stalks develop, until you have the plants buried to within a few inches of the tip of their leaves.
passages.plain: Sow early celery seeds in a hotbed. Move the seedlings to a cold frame. Keep them there until May. Then plant them in your richest soil. Space them six inches apart in a row. Blanch the plants by putting up boards. These boards should be one foot wide on each side of the row. Leave a three inch opening at the top so the plants get a little light. For late and winter use, sow the seeds in open ground in May. Blanch them by earthing up the soil gradually as the stalks grow. Bury the plants until they are only a few inches below the tips of their leaves.

passages.old: Use clean, dry soil in banking the plants. Sawdust is good, but care must be taken to make use of a kind that does not have a strong odor. Pinedust will give the plants a disagreeable flavor. For winter use, take up plants, root and all, and pack close together in boxes and store in a cool, dark cellar. White Plume is the best early variety. Giant Pascal is probably the most satisfactory winter variety, but Winter Queen is a favorite with many. Both are so tender and have such a rich, nutty flavor that it is not an easy matter to decide between them.
passages.plain: Use clean and dry soil to bank the plants. Sawdust is good. You must choose a kind that does not have a strong smell. Pine dust will give the plants a bad flavor. For winter use, take up the plants with their roots. Pack them close together in boxes. Store them in a cool and dark cellar. White Plume is the best early variety. Giant Pascal is probably the best winter variety. Winter Queen is also a favorite for many people. Both are very tender and have a rich, nutty flavor. It is hard to choose between them.

passages.old: Cucumber For very early cucumbers plant the seed in the hotbed in March or April, but do not put the plants into the garden until all danger of frost is over. 'This plant requires a rich and mellow soil. It should be set in hills at least four feet apart. It is a good plan to start the seed in pieces of sod placed grass-side down. This enables one to move them from the hotbed without any disturbance of their roots. 'The cucumber- or squash-beetle often destroys the plants when they are put in the open ground if close watch is not taken and prompt effort made to rout the enemy.
passages.plain: Plant cucumber seeds in a hotbed in March or April. Do not put the plants in the garden until the danger of frost is over. This plant needs rich and mellow soil. Place the plants in hills at least four feet apart. It is a good plan to start the seeds in pieces of sod placed grass side down. This lets you move them from the hotbed without disturbing the roots. The cucumber or squash beetle often destroys the plants when you put them in the open ground. You must watch them closely and work quickly to drive away the enemy.

passages.old: Spray with Nicoticide infusion, taking pains to have it reach the under side of the leaves. Dry road-dust sifted thickly over the plants is often found quite effective, but because of the inability to apply it to the under side of the leaves the liquid insecticide will be found more effective. Improved Early White Spine is a favorite with all who like a crisp, tender-meated, finely flavored cucumber. Ever-bearing is an excellent sort for pickling as well as for use on the table during the fall, as it continues to bear until frost kills the vines.
passages.plain: Spray the plants with a Nicoticide mixture. Make sure the liquid reaches the bottom of the leaves. You can also use thick dry road dust on the plants. This is often effective. However, liquid insecticide is better because you can spray it on the bottom of the leaves. Improved Early White Spine is a popular choice. People like it because it has crisp, tender meat and a good flavor. Ever-bearing is a great variety for pickling. You can also eat it at the table during the fall. It keeps producing fruit until the frost kills the vines.

passages.old: Corn Sweet-corn is one of the most delicious of all garden vegetables, and every garden that is large enough to admit of its culture should give place to two or three varieties of it. Because of its tall growth and the distance required between rows it is not adapted to culture in the very small garden, though I would willingly go without some of the other vegetables generally grown there in order to give place to a few hills of it. Golden Bantam produces ears only four or five inches in length, but what they lack in size they make up for in tenderness and sweetness.
passages.plain: Sweet-corn is one of the most delicious garden vegetables. Every garden large enough to grow it should have two or three varieties. Corn grows tall and needs space between the rows. This means it is not good for very small gardens. However, you could choose to remove some other vegetables to make room for a few rows of corn. The Golden Bantam variety produces ears that are only four or five inches long. These ears are very tender and sweet even though they are small.

passages.old: Country Gentleman is a medium variety, very tender, sweet, and juicy. But the ideal sweet-corn is Stowell's Evergreen. No other variety equals it in tenderness, sugary sweetness, and rich flavor. It does not come to maturity until quite late in the season, but it remains in excellent eatingcondition until the plant is killed by frost. Do not plant until the weather and the ground are warm, generally about May 10th at the extreme North. Sweet-corn seed often decays if put into the ground as early as field-corn. Have the soil rich and mellow, and cultivate frequently and thoroughly.
passages.plain: Country Gentleman is a medium variety of sweet corn. It is very tender, sweet, and juicy. However, Stowell's Evergreen is the ideal sweet corn. No other variety is as tender, sugary, or flavorful. It does not reach maturity until late in the season. It stays in good eating condition until the frost kills the plant. Do not plant until the weather and the ground are warm. This usually happens around May 10th in the far North. Sweet-corn seed often rots if you put it in the ground as early as field-corn. Keep the soil rich and mellow. Cultivate the soil frequently and thoroughly.

passages.old: If a dry spell comes along make use of the cultivator daily until the drought is broken. Endive This plant ought to be grown far more extensively than it is because it is one of the best salad plants we have for fall and winter use. Some should be sown in April for use during the summer, and some in July, for late use. When the plants are two or three inches high transplant to rich soil, setting them about ten inches apart. When nearly full-grown, gather the leaves together and tie them with strips of cloth, thus excluding the light from the central part of the bunch.
passages.plain: Use a cultivator every day if there is a dry spell until the drought ends. You should grow more endive because it is one of the best salad plants for fall and winter. Sow some seeds in April to use during the summer. Sow some seeds in July for late use. Move the plants to rich soil when they are two or three inches high. Space them about ten inches apart. When the plants are almost full grown, gather the leaves together. Tie them with strips of cloth. This blocks the light from the middle of the bunch.

passages.old: It must be blanched before it is fit for table use. - This part of the work must be done while the plants are perfectly dry. If done | when they are wet or even moist, they will be quite sure to rot. Lettuce This plant should be started in the hotbed if there is one. The seedlings should be transferred to the cold-frame before they have attained much size, and left there until the ground becomes warm. Very fine lettuce, however, can be grown from seed sown directly in the open ground about the first of May, if the soil is warm and rich.
passages.plain: You must blanch this part before you can eat it. You must do this work while the plants are completely dry. If you do it when they are wet or damp, they will rot. You should start lettuce in a hotbed if you have one. You should move the seedlings to a cold frame before they get big. Leave them there until the ground gets warm. You can also grow very fine lettuce by sowing seeds directly in the open ground. Do this around the first of May if the soil is warm and rich.

passages.old: A fertile soil is quite important, as 1t 1s necessary to bring on a rapid growth in order to have the plant crisp and tender. Slow development gives a comparatively worthless article. The All Heart variety is excellent for spring and early summer use. It forms a solid head, and is very crisp and tender, with that rich, buttery flavor that the lover of this plant insists on. Mammoth Salamander is one of the best late-season kinds. M elons These, like corn and cabbage, are not adapted to culture in the small garden because they require more room than it is possible to give them without giving up other vegetables which the housewife cannot well afford to go without.
passages.plain: Fertile soil is very important. You need it to make plants grow quickly. Fast growth makes the plants crisp and tender. Slow growth makes them less valuable. The All Heart variety is great for spring and early summer. It makes a solid head. It is very crisp and tender. It has a rich and buttery flavor that people who love this plant want. Mammoth Salamander is one of the best types for late season. Melons are like corn and cabbage. They are not good for small gardens. They need more room than you can give them. If you give them more room, you would have to give up other vegetables. A housewife cannot easily do without those other vegetables.

passages.old: But in good-sized gardens I would advise their culture, because there is nothing else quite equal to them in delicacy of flavor and luscious sweetness. They require a light, rich soil. Plant when the ground is warm, and not before, in hills four feet apart. It is a good plan to put a generous quantity of manure from the henhouse in each hill, working it well into the soil before seed is planted. Put at least a dozen seed in each hill, for some of the seedlings will doubtless be destroyed by the beetle that works on cucumber- and squash-vines.
passages.plain: I recommend growing them in large gardens. Nothing else has a flavor as delicate or a sweetness as delicious as they do. They need soil that is light and rich. You should plant them when the ground is warm. Do not plant them before then. Space the hills four feet apart. It is a good plan to put a large amount of manure from the henhouse in each hill. Mix the manure well into the soil before you plant the seeds. Put at least twelve seeds in each hill. Some of the seedlings will likely be destroyed by the beetle that attacks cucumber and squash vines.

passages.old: All the varieties named are of superior flavor, very productive, and sure to give complete satisfaction. passages.plain: All the varieties listed have great flavor and produce a lot. They will satisfy you completely. You should sow radishes early. You can plant them in a hotbed or in the open ground. passages.plain: Cardinal Globe is the standard early variety of radish. Crimson Giant is a variety that matures a little later. Both types are crisp, tender, and juicy. These qualities make radishes a popular choice. Icicle is a white variety that takes a long time to grow. It is very crisp and brittle. This variety stays fresh for use longer than any other variety. Rhubarb is another plant. It likes soil that is deep, rich, and moist. You should plant it in permanent beds. Space the plants about three feet apart. Do not try to grow rhubarb from seed. You should get roots that are one or two years old.

passages.old: Victoria is a standard variety. Salsify A vegetable that ought to be grown a great deal more than it is. Being hardy, it can be left in the ground over winter, or it can be dug and stored in the cellar along with parsnips and carrots for use in winter. Sow early. Squash Probably the best variety of 'summer squash for home use is Giant Crook Neck.
passages.plain: Victoria is a standard variety. Salsify is a vegetable that you should grow much more than people do now. Its popular name is vegetable oyster. This name is correct because it has a clear oyster flavor. Many people prefer it to actual oysters when it is cooked correctly. It is hardy. You can leave it in the ground over the winter. You can also dig it up and store it in a cellar with parsnips and carrots to use in the winter. Sow it early. Giant Crook Neck is probably the best variety of summer squash for home use.

passages.old: For winter use the Hubbard stands at the head of the list. These favorite vegetables require a rich soil. They should be planted in hills about three feet apart. Have the soil rich. As they become larger they can be sprayed with the Nicoticide infusion heretofore spoken of. Spinach Desirable for "'greens." Sow as early in the spring as the ground is in good working condition.

passages.plain: Make sure the soil is very rich to encourage soft and juicy growth. Plant seeds one month apart for a continuous supply. The Long-Season variety is the best one I know of. You must start the plants as early as March to get a very early crop. Move the plants from the hotbed to a cold frame when they are three or four inches high. Do not put them in the open ground until there is no more danger from frost.

chapters.title: Small fruits and their culture

passages.old: UITE as important as garden vegetables is the small-fruit department of each home that is living up to its privileges. Of course there will be no room for raspberries and blackberries on the little home lot, but one can have a row of strawberries there, in almost all cases, and a few currant-bushes can be tucked away in nooks and corners where quite likely nothing else would be grown if the tiny space were not given up to There are places all over the country where a collection of small fruit ought to be grown, but which are without it.
passages.plain: Small fruits are as important as garden vegetables for a home that is doing well. You cannot grow raspberries and blackberries on a small home lot. However, you can grow a row of strawberries in almost all cases. You can also put a few currant bushes in corners. You would likely not grow anything else in those small spaces if you did not use them for berries. There are many places across the country where people should grow small fruit but do not.

passages.old: Why? There are several answers to the question. One is: Neglect to live up to the possibilities of the place because of carelessness, or possibly because the owner is distrustful of his ability to grow them successfully. Another is: The impression that these plants are so exacting in their demands that none but skilled gardeners are warranted in undertaking their culture. And a third one is: The uncertainty of being unable to take them through our severe Northern winters safely. The first objection is met with the argument that the man who is obliged to work for a living, and has a family to support, has no excuse for neglecting to avail himself and those dependent on him of all the good things that can be grown from the plants named, if he owns a piece of ground large enough to accommodate a small collection.
passages.plain: Why do people not grow these vegetables? There are several reasons. One reason is that people are careless or they do not trust their own ability to grow them. Another reason is the idea that these plants are so difficult that only skilled gardeners can grow them. A third reason is the fear that the plants will not survive the harsh Northern winters. You can answer the first objection with an argument. A man who must work for a living and support a family has no excuse for not growing these plants. He should provide these good things for himself and his family if he owns enough land for a small collection.

passages.old: The second objection is not justified, because it is an easy matter for any man to learn how to care for small fruits if he sets about it with the intention of mastering its details. There is really no basis in fact for the third one, for we have, to-day, varieties of each kind of small fruit-that are entirely hardy at the North if properly cared for in the fall. There should be a strawberry-bed, large or small, in every garden, if I had my way about it. Here I suppose some reader will meet me with the objection that ''strawberries don't pay.
passages.plain: The second objection is not correct. It is easy for any person to learn how to care for small fruits. You just need to study the details. The third objection is also not true. Today, we have varieties of every small fruit. These fruits can survive in the North if you care for them properly in the fall. I believe every garden should have a strawberry bed, whether it is large or small. Some readers might tell me that strawberries do not make money.

passages.old: 'They require too much care, and the beds soon run out, and then everything has to be done over again." Now I claim that strawberries do pay if they get the right kind of treatment. No one has a right to expect much from them if he simply sticks a plant into the soil and leaves it to take care of itself thereafter. Strawberries cultivated in this manner don't pay, I admit. And it is well that they do not, for no one has a right' to expect much, if anything, from a plant of any kind that he isn't willing to take good care of.
passages.plain: Some people say strawberries require too much care. They say the beds run out quickly and then you have to start over. I believe that strawberries will be profitable if you give them the right treatment. You cannot expect much from them if you just put a plant in the soil and let it take care of itself. I admit that strawberries grown this way do not pay. It is good that they do not. You have no right to expect anything from any plant if you are not willing to take good care of it.

passages.old: While the strawberry will not take care of itself, it really requires no more attention than most other crops. And as to "'running out," that cuts no figure, when you come to think about it, because ''doing things al! over again'? amounts to no more than planting vegetables each season. This has to be done yearly, and strawberries will demand only annual attention, thus putting the two classes of plants on practically the same basis. I am aware that some writers on strawberry culture have ventilated a good many far-fetched ideas of their own in print relative to the eulture of this plant, and so elaborate and complicated are some of these theories that many an amateur has, after reading them, abandoned the idea of having a strawberry-bed.
passages.plain: Strawberries do not take care of themselves. However, they do not need more attention than most other crops. Some people worry about the work of starting over. But doing things again is just like planting vegetables every season. You must do this every year. Strawberries only need your attention once a year. This makes them about the same as other plants. Some writers have shared many strange ideas about growing strawberries. Some of these theories are very complicated. Many beginners gave up on planting strawberries after reading those books.

passages.old: But it is a fact susceptible of proof by any man who gives it a trial that strawberry culture may be made a success without adopting the views of persons who seem to think that theory is more important than common sense. The simplest method of strawberry-growing that I know anything about is what is called the ''one-crop system." Set the plants in rows three feet apart, to allow the use of the cultivator between them. Let the plants be a foot apart in the row. Keep the ground between the rows well cultivated, and in the second summer, when the plants are bearing their first crop of fruit, allow them to send their runners into the space between the rows and take root there.
passages.plain: You can prove that growing strawberries is successful without following people who think theory is more important than common sense. The simplest method I know is the one-crop system. Place the plants in rows that are three feet apart. This space allows you to use a cultivator between the rows. Place the plants one foot apart within each row. Keep the ground between the rows well cultivated. During the second summer, the plants will produce their first crop of fruit. At that time, let the plants send their runners into the space between the rows. Let the runners take root there.

passages.old: When these young plants have fully established themselves, which will be by the end of August, as a general thing, take a spade and cut down between them and the old plants. Then dig up the old plants, making the place where they grew a space between rows. Next season train runners from the bearing plants back into the old row. By thus alternating the location of the plants you keep the garden supplied with one-year-old ones from which you get but one crop of fruit. This method is so simple that any one can understand it, and it has the indorsement of some of our most up-to-date gardeners who recognize the fact that one full crop of berries is about all that can be expected from the strawberry.
passages.plain: Wait until these young plants are fully established. This usually happens by the end of August. Take a spade and cut the ground between the young plants and the old plants. Dig up the old plants. This creates a space between the rows. Next season, grow runners from the bearing plants back into the old row. You do this by switching the location of the plants. This keeps your garden supplied with one-year-old plants. You only get one crop of fruit from these plants. This method is simple for anyone to understand. Modern gardeners support this method. They know that you can only expect one full crop of berries from a strawberry plant.

passages.old: Of course older plants will bear fruit, but never of the quantity and quality which is obtained from strong, healthy young plants whose vitality has not been.drawn upon by the production of a heavy first crop. This one-crop system makes it possible to grow fine berries without giving the plants more care than is required by ordinary vegetables. The soil for strawberries should be rich and mellow, and should be kept entirely free from weeds. It is a good plan to spread clean straw between the rows before the crop ripens, to keep the fruit from coming in contact with the ground or having sand washed upon it 'by heavy rains.
passages.plain: Older plants will produce fruit. However, they will not produce as much or as high-quality fruit as strong, healthy young plants. Young plants are better because they have not used up their energy by growing a heavy first crop. This one-crop system lets you grow great berries. You do not have to give them more care than you give normal vegetables. The soil for strawberries must be rich and soft. You must keep the soil completely free of weeds. It is a good plan to spread clean straw between the rows before the fruit ripens. This keeps the fruit from touching the ground. It also stops heavy rains from washing sand onto the fruit.

passages.old: The best variety of strawberry that I have ever grown is Brandywine. It is very productive, bears large berries, has a most delicious flavor, and is never hollow-hearted. It ripens in mid-season. The best late variety, allowing me to be judge, is Gandy. This kind requires a very rich soil. Where it can be given this, no more satisfactory ae can be grown, The two varieties named above combine all the best qualities of this most popular fruit. Several times in the last few years the announcement has been made that a fall-bearing strawberry has been produced, but as it was of European origin it did not prove satisfactory under American conditions.
passages.plain: The best strawberry variety I have ever grown is Brandywine. It produces many large berries. It has a delicious flavor and the berries are never hollow. It ripens in the middle of the season. The best late variety is Gandy. This variety needs very rich soil. If you give it rich soil, you cannot grow a better variety. These two varieties have all the best qualities of this popular fruit. People have announced a fall-bearing strawberry several times in the last few years. However, that strawberry was from Europe. It did not work well in American conditions.

passages.old: Of late, however, some of our most progressive smallfruit growers have succeeded in growing two varieties that promise to be really good fallcroppers. 'These produce, if allowed to do so, their main crop at the same time as other varieties, and keep on bearing until frost. But in order to secure a good crop late in the season it is advisable to cut away all buds that appear in June, keeping the strength of the plant in reserve for the fall crop. It is well to mulch these plants during the hot, dry weather of summer.
passages.plain: Some modern smallfruit growers have successfully grown two varieties that produce good crops in the fall. These plants produce their main crop at the same time as other varieties if you let them. They keep producing fruit until the first frost. To get a good crop late in the season, you should cut away all the buds that appear in June. This keeps the strength of the plant for the fall crop. You should mulch these plants during the hot and dry summer weather.

passages.old: 'These fall-bearing varieties are on the market under the names of Superb and Progressive. The blackberry responds generously to good treatment, bearing enormous quantities of large, juicy berries of most delicious flavor when given proper care. It prefers a rather sandy soil. In order to secure a fresh stock of wood for each season's Pop: the old canes should be cut away as soon as they have ripened their fruit, thus throwing all the strength of the plant into the production of new canes from which fruit is to be expected next sea- While the two leading varieties, Kittatinny and Snyder, are quite hardy, it is well to take the precaution of giving them some protection to guard against the possible loss of some of the unripened growth of the season.
passages.plain: You can find these fall-bearing varieties on the market under the names Superb and Progressive. The blackberry produces many large and juicy berries with a delicious flavor if you give it proper care. It prefers soil that is somewhat sandy. To make sure you have fresh wood for each season, you should cut away the old canes as soon as they finish ripening their fruit. This lets the plant put all its strength into growing new canes for next year's fruit. The two main varieties are Kittatinny and Snyder. These two are very hardy. However, you should still protect them to prevent losing some of the fruit that has not ripened yet.

passages.old: This, is done to the best advantage by removing two or three spadefuls of soil from the base of each plant, close to its roots, and then tipping the bush over until it les flat on the ground. This could not be done without running the risk of breaking some of the stiff and brittle canes if the excavation were not made. When the bushes are spread out on the ground, where they are held in place by laying boards across them, throw some coarse litter over the base of the plant, and scatter a covering of straw over the branches.
passages.plain: You should do this by removing two or three spadefuls of soil from the base of each plant near its roots. Then, tip the bush over until it lies flat on the ground. You must dig the soil out first so you do not break the stiff and brittle canes. When the bushes are spread out on the ground, hold them in place by laying boards across them. Throw some coarse litter over the base of the plant. Scatter a covering of straw over the branches.

passages.old: As soon as the frost is out of the ground in the spring, lift the bushes and replace the soil that was taken away in the fall. Raspberries are second only to strawberries in deliciousness of flavor, and should have a place in all gardens where there is room for them. They do well in almost all soils, if well drained. A sandy loam, however, is the soil that seems to suit them best. Their old canes, like those of the blackberry, should be cut away at the end of the fruiting season.
passages.plain: Lift the bushes as soon as the frost leaves the ground in the spring. Replace the soil that you took away in the fall. Raspberries are the second most delicious fruit after strawberries. They should be in every garden that has enough room for them. They grow well in almost all soils if the water drains well. Sandy loam is the soil that suits them best. You should cut away their old canes at the end of the fruiting season. This is the same time you cut the canes of the blackberry.

passages.old: Cuthbert is the leading red variety. Cumberland is the favorite black kind. I notice that one of our most prominent growers of small fruit offers an ever-bearing raspberry this season, under the name of Red Ranere. I have no knowledge of its merits other than that which I gain from the grower's announcement in introducing this sort to the market, but from intimate personal acquaintance with the man I am quite confident that the plant must possess real merit, for he is not a person given to exaggeration. I quote from what he has to say in reference to this variety in a leading horticultural magazine: This is not only the earliest red raspberry, but it is a perpetual fruiting one.
passages.plain: Cuthbert is the main red variety. Cumberland is the favorite black variety. One of our most famous small fruit growers is selling an ever-bearing raspberry this season. He calls it Red Ranere. I do not know its qualities except for what the grower said when he put it on the market. However, I know the man personally. I am sure the plant is good because he does not exaggerate. He said the following about this variety in a top gardening magazine. It is the earliest red raspberry. It is also a variety that produces fruit all year long.

passages.old: Its main crop is greater than that of any other variety I grow. It continues to bear on its old canes until late in August, at about which time the canes of the season's growth come into bearing. These produce a large amount of fine fruit until late in the fall. The berries are very attractive, being a bright, rich crimson. They are of good size, and of very superior quality, with a rich, sugary, full raspberry Sh A-B-C OF VEGETABLE GARDENING | I would advise the amateur gardener to give this variety a trial.
passages.plain: This variety produces more fruit than any other variety I grow. It keeps producing fruit on its old canes until late August. Around that time, the canes that grew during the current season start to produce fruit. These produce a large amount of high quality fruit until late fall. The berries are very attractive. They are a bright and rich crimson color. They are a good size and have a very superior quality. They have a rich and sugary raspberry flavor. I advise you to try this variety if you are an amateur gardener.

passages.old: Raspberries late in the fall would be thoroughly appreciated by those with whom this fruit is a favorite. The currant is one of the garden's indispensables. It furnishes us with fruit of just the right degree of tart acidity to fit the season in which it is at its prime, and who does not get a deal of enjoyment out of a greencurrant pie? No kind of small fruit is easier to grow successfully. Worms frequently attack the bushes in spring, and often ruin the crop unless steps are taken to put a prompt end to their depredations, but spraying with Nicoticide infusion will rout them in most cases.
passages.plain: You will enjoy raspberries late in the fall if you love this fruit. Currants are a must-have for your garden. They provide fruit with the perfect amount of tart acidity for the season. You can enjoy a greencurrant pie. No small fruit is easier to grow successfully. Worms often attack the bushes in the spring. They can ruin the crop unless you stop them quickly. Spraying with a Nicoticide infusion will drive them away in most cases.

passages.plain: I advise you to buy a few plants of this variety and try them out. You should not ignore the gooseberry. Many people say the bush gets mildew so badly that the crop usually fails. passages.plain: You can plant all kinds of small fruit in the spring. This is better than planting in the fall. A nurseryman might tell you that it does not matter much if you plant in the spring or the fall. The writer tried both methods. He was most successful when he put plants out in April and May.
