chapters.title: Hotbeds and coldframes

passages.old: N order to have vegetables early in the season it will be necessary to give them a start some weeks before the ground is in proper condition for the reception of seed. Sometimes this is done by sowing the seed in pots and boxes in the living-room, as advised in Chapter VI, but here conditions are not very favorable to healthy growth, unless great care is taken to follow the directions given in the chapter mentioned, and even then success does not always attend our efforts. In order to give our plants the early start that they must have if we want vegetables at a time when most gardeners are getting the garden ready for planting, we must make use of the hotbed.
passages.plain: You need to start your vegetables several weeks before the ground is ready for seeds if you want to harvest them early. You can sometimes sow seeds in pots and boxes in your living room. This is explained in Chapter VI. However, the living room is not a very good place for healthy growth. You must follow the directions in that chapter very carefully. Even then, you might not always succeed. To give your plants the early start they need, you must use a hotbed. This allows you to grow them while most other gardeners are just preparing their gardens for planting.

passages.old: If this is done we can gain from six weeks to two months in time, and have lettuce and radishes before our neighbors who are without hotbed facilities consider it safe to put seed into the ground. | At the North the first of March is quite early enough to get the hotbed under way. I am aware that many young gardeners have the impression that a hotbed is, in some respects, a mysterious thing, and because of this they do not undertake to make one. Now there is nothing simpler than a hotbed when you come to a study of it.
passages.plain: You can save between six weeks and two months of time by doing this. You will have lettuce and radishes before your neighbors. Your neighbors do not have hotbeds. They wait until they think it is safe to put seeds in the ground. In the North, March 1 is early enough to start a hotbed. Many young gardeners think a hotbed is mysterious. Because of this, they do not try to build one. A hotbed is actually very simple when you study it.

passages.old: It is simply making a place in which summer conditions can be imitated by supplying it with steady, gentle heat, and in confining this heat within an inclosure. The heat is generated by the use of material which ferments, and the inclosure is nothing but a combination of boards and glass so arranged that the temperature inside it can be regulated to suit the requirements of the plants you undertake to grow in it. The heat-generating material is generally fresh manure from the horse-stable, or a mixture of that and coarse litter.
passages.plain: You are simply making a place that mimics summer conditions. You do this by providing steady and gentle heat and keeping that heat inside an enclosure. You create the heat by using material that ferments. The enclosure is a combination of boards and glass. You arrange these parts so you can control the temperature for the plants you want to grow. The material that creates heat is usually fresh manure from a horse stable or a mixture of manure and coarse litter.

passages.old: Because the heat from rapid fermentation is quite intense, at first the material from which it is obtained should be prepared before the hotbed is brought into use. A quantity of it should be spread on the site selected for the hotbed, which should be one that is high and dry, covering a space larger than the hotbed frame is to be. Spread it in layers four or five inches deep, tramping each layer down well. When there is a foot and a half of it, cover it with something that will shed rain, and wait for fermentation to take place.
passages.plain: The heat from fast fermentation is very strong. You must prepare the material before you use the hotbed. Choose a site that is high and dry. Spread the material over this site. The area must be larger than the hotbed frame. Spread the material in layers that are four or five inches deep. Trample each layer down well. When you have a foot and a half of material, cover it with something that sheds rain. Wait for fermentation to happen.

passages.old: A warm moisture will rise from it like steam. After two or three days fork the material over, and remove all straw, and make another heap similar to the first one, taking great pains to have it firm and compact. It is very important that it should have considerable solidity, as a heap of loose litter will never give satisfactory results. There should be at least a foot and a half of this heat-generating material. While waiting for fermentation to take place in the manure-pile, prepare the frame for your hotbed.
passages.plain: Warm moisture will rise from the pile like steam. After two or three days, turn the material over with a fork. Remove all the straw. Make a new heap similar to the first one. Work hard to make it firm and compact. It is very important that the pile is solid. A heap of loose litter will not give good results. You must have at least a foot and a half of this heat-generating material. While you wait for the manure pile to ferment, prepare the frame for your hotbed.

passages.old: Let it be about a foot and a half in depth at the back, and eight or ten inches deep in front, with sides that slope from the wider boards to the narrower ones. Cover it with glass set in sash. If possible have the sash hinged to the back-board, so that it can be lifted for ventilation without removing it. The best location for a hotbed is one facing the south, that all possible advantage can. be taken of sunshine, and against a building or fence that will protect it on the north from cold winds.
passages.plain: Make the back of the bed about one and a half feet deep. Make the front eight or ten inches deep. The sides should slope from the wider boards to the narrower ones. Cover the bed with glass in a sash. If you can, attach hinges to the back board. This lets you lift the sash for air without taking it off. Put the hotbed in a spot facing south. This helps you get as much sunshine as possible. Place it against a building or a fence. This will protect the bed from cold winds coming from the north.

passages.old: Some persons prefer to make an excavation a foot or more in depth for the reception of the heating material, but this is not a matter of much importance. As a general thing it will not be possible to do this in a satisfactory manner while there is frost in the ground, as there will be at the North until after the first of March. | When the first stages of fermentation are over, set the hotbed frame in place, and fill in with five or six inches of very fine, rich soil.
passages.plain: Some people prefer to dig a hole one foot deep or more for the heating material. This is not very important. You generally cannot do this well while the ground is frozen. In the North, the ground stays frozen until after March 1. When the first stages of fermentation are finished, put the hotbed frame in place. Fill it with five or six inches of very fine, rich soil.

passages.old: This is what your seed is to be planted The young gardener will be surprised at the amount of heat contained in an inclosure like the one described. It will be very similar to the weather conditions of early or middle May out of doors. In it plants will grow healthily and vigorously, provided they are given plenty of fresh air. This 1s a matter of the greatest importance. Unless your seedlings are aired daily, if the weather is pleasant, they will make a rapid but weak growth, and when the time comes to put them in the cold-frame or the open ground, provided they are alive then, they will be so lacking in vitality that the change will be pretty sure to put an end to them.
passages.plain: This is where you should plant your seeds. A new gardener might be surprised by how much heat a structure like this holds. The conditions inside will feel like the weather in early or middle May outside. Plants will grow healthy and strong in this space as long as you give them plenty of fresh air. This is very important. If you do not air your seedlings every day when the weather is nice, they will grow fast but weak. When it is time to move them to a cold frame or the open ground, they might die. If they are still alive, they will lack the strength to survive the change.

passages.old: On every 6 rai sunny or warm day the sash should be lifted _ an inch or two, about ten o'clock, and left in that condition until about two. Care must be taken, however, to see that the wind does not blow from a quarter that will drive the cold air in upon the plants. The admission of a cold blast will often - fatal to the tender plants. Great caution must be cca in regard to ventilation. 'The aim should be, at all times, to admit pure, fresh air without allowing cold to enter with it.
passages.plain: On every sunny or warm day, you should lift the sash one or two inches at about ten o'clock. Leave it in that position until about two o'clock. You must be careful that the wind does not blow from a direction that pushes cold air onto the plants. A cold blast can often kill tender plants. You must use great caution with ventilation. Your goal should always be to let in pure, fresh air without letting cold air enter with it.

passages.old: This may seem a somewhat paradoxical statement, for at first thought it will seem impossible for air from without to come in without taking along with it the cold air which is in circulation outside, but when one takes into consideration the fact that the warm air inside the hotbed meets the air from out of doors at the point of entrance it will be understood that it repels or counteracts it to an extent that makes it safe to open the sash slightly when the outside temperature is nearly down to freezing-point.
passages.plain: This might sound strange. You might think it is impossible for outside air to enter without bringing in the cold air from outdoors. However, you must consider how the warm air inside the hotbed meets the outside air at the entrance. The warm air pushes back against the cold air. This makes it safe for you to open the sash slightly even when the outside temperature is almost at the freezing point.

passages.old: 'The hotbed-owner must study existing conditions and be governed accordingly. It is impossible to lay down any hard-and-fast rules to apply in this case. On cold nights the hotbed sash should be covered with blankets or old carpeting to prevent the formation of frost on the glass. If you find, in the morning, that the glass is covered with moisture on its under side, raise the sash a trifle and leave it so until the moisture clears away. If at any time you have reason to ae that the warmth inside the frame is decreasing too rapidly, bank up about it with fresh fermenting material.
passages.plain: You must study the current conditions of your hotbed and follow what they tell you. You cannot follow strict rules for this task. On cold nights, cover the hotbed sash with blankets or old carpets. This stops frost from forming on the glass. If you see moisture on the inside of the glass in the morning, lift the sash a little bit. Leave it that way until the moisture goes away. If you think the heat inside the frame is dropping too fast, pile fresh fermenting material around it.

passages.old: After constructing the hotbed and putting the frame and sash in place, test the heat inside by an accurate thermometer before venturing to sow any seed. When it registers 85° or 90° the bed is ready for seeding. In making the frame for a hotbed eare should be taken to see that all joints fit snugly. A great deal of cold can be admitted through a very small crevice. A few cracks will let out the heat faster than it is generated, therefore see to it that in constructing the frame a good piece of work is done. - Some persons tell me that they always bank up a hotbed with earth.
passages.plain: Build the hotbed and put the frame and sash in place. Test the heat inside with an accurate thermometer before you plant any seeds. The bed is ready for seeds when it shows 85 degrees or 90 degrees. When you make the frame for a hotbed, make sure all joints fit tightly together. A lot of cold air can enter through a very small crack. A few cracks will let heat out faster than the bed can make it. You must do good work when building the frame. Some people tell me that they always cover a hotbed with earth.

passages.old: This enables it to retain the heat better than it is possible for it to do without banking. A hotbed will be of no particular benefit unless supplemented by a cold-frame. 'This is simply a snug inclosure of boards covered with glass, into which plants from the hotbed are to be set for the purpose of hardening them off before they are put into the open ground. In other words, it is a hotbed without heat. The temperature in it ought to register from 60° to 65°. Raise the sash an inch or two on sunny days before the rays of the sun striking on the glass raise the temperature inside to a degree too intense for the good of your plants.
passages.plain: This helps the bed keep heat better than it can without banking. A hotbed is not very helpful unless you also use a cold frame. A cold frame is a small area made of boards and covered with glass. You put plants from the hotbed into this frame to harden them before you move them into the open ground. You can think of it as a hotbed without heat. The temperature inside should be between 60 and 65 degrees. On sunny days, lift the sash one or two inches. Do this before the sun hits the glass and makes the inside too hot for your plants.

passages.old: It will be readily understood from what I have said above that in order to attain success in the management of a hotbed great care will have to be exercised at all times and frequent attention given. It is not a selfregulating thing by any means. You will have to consider the weather, the time of day when ventilation should be given, frequency of watering, and other matters which cannot be touched on here because of a more or less local character. Plants in the hotbed should be watered cautiously.
passages.plain: You must be very careful and pay close attention to your hotbed at all times to be successful. It does not manage itself. You must think about the weather. You must decide what time of day to provide ventilation. You must decide how often to water the plants. You must also consider other matters that depend on your local area. You should water the plants in the hotbed carefully.

passages.old: An oversupply will often cause the seedlings to ''damp off,' and 'a lack of sufficient moisture at the roots will speedily result in injury, if not death. Whenever water is applied, use a sprinkler that throws a fine spray. If thrown on the soil in a stream the water will often wash the smaller plants out of place. It may puzzle one to tell when just enough has been given. 'This is best determined by an examination of the soil. If moderately moist there is plenty of moisture below.
passages.plain: Too much water will often cause the seedlings to damp off. A lack of enough moisture at the roots will quickly cause injury or death. You should use a sprinkler that gives a fine spray whenever you water. If you pour water in a stream on the soil, it will often wash the smaller plants out of place. You might wonder when you have given just enough water. You can best determine this by checking the soil. If the soil is moderately moist, there is plenty of moisture below.

chapters.why: The principles of using controlled environments to extend the growing season remain fundamental for early vegetable production.

chapters.title: Small gardens

passages.old: ANY persons who would like to grow flowers and vegetables do not attempt to grow any because they do not consider that they have a place large enough to justify them in doing so. Here is where they make a mistake. A garden need not be a large one to be enjoyable. A few plants are better than none. It is possible to make a bit of garden more satisfactory than a large one because it will be more likely to get more attention than would be given to the larger one, and attention is one of the important features of any successful garden.
passages.plain: You might want to grow flowers and vegetables but think you do not have enough space. You are making a mistake. A garden does not have to be large to be enjoyable. Having a few plants is better than having none. You can make a small garden more successful than a large one. This is because you will give a small garden more attention. Attention is one of the important parts of a successful garden.

passages.old: There will, in the majority of cases, be little nooks and corners here and there about the home grounds in which some plants can be grown by those disposed to make the most of existing conditions. These, if not improved, will be pretty sure to be given over to weeds, or to the accumulation of rubbish of one kind or another, and they will detract from the tidy and clean appearance which should characterize the home everywhere. If the owners of these bits of ground, these possibilities for adding to the attractiveness of home, could be made to realize the amount of pleasure they could be made to afford with very little exertion on their part, the general work of civic improvement societies would be most beneficial, and this would be done at the very place where civic improvement ought to start, the home.
passages.plain: Most homes have small corners or spots where you can grow plants. You can use these spaces if you want to make the most of what you already have. If you do not improve these spots, they will likely fill with weeds or trash. This will make your home look messy. You can make these areas much more beautiful with very little effort. If you realize how much pleasure these spots can bring you, it would help the work of civic improvement societies. This work should start at your own home.

passages.old: 'There can be no real and lasting improvement in civic undertaking unless the individual home takes up the matter. The civic improvement society that starts out with the idea of improving things generally, but does not begin the good work at the home is working on the idea of making clean the outside of the cup and ignoring the condition inside it. Just as the home is the foundation of society, so must it be made the pivotal point at which any substantial and lasting improvement finds its beginning. Because the scattered places about the small home in which few plants could be grown will not admit of bed-making, or the "designs"? which many persons seem to think indispensable in gardening, 1s no good reason why we should not take advantage of and make the most of them.
passages.plain: You cannot make real and lasting improvements to a city unless you start at your own home. A society that tries to improve things in general but does not start at home is like someone cleaning the outside of a cup while ignoring the inside. The home is the foundation of society. It must be the starting point for any big and lasting improvement. You might think the small spaces around your home are too small to grow plants or make garden beds. You might also think you need special designs to garden. There is no good reason why you should not use these small spaces and make the most of them.

passages.old: If one lives in a community where there are German families he will be surprised at the amount of vegetables they grow in each home-lot. Not an inch of soil is allowed to go to waste. A large amount of the food of the family is erown in places which most Americans would overlook, simply because of the prevailing idea that unless one can do things on a large scale it is not worth while to attempt doing anything. The German has been brought up to not ''despise the day of small things," and he profits by the advice.
passages.plain: You will be surprised if you live in a community with German families. You will see that they grow many vegetables on every home lot. They do not let any soil go to waste. They grow a large amount of their food in places that most Americans would ignore. Most Americans think it is not worth doing something unless they can do it on a large scale. The German person was raised not to look down on small things. He benefits from this advice.

passages.old: As we might, if we would, and, I am glad to say, as more and more are profiting by year by year as they become aware of the fact that much can be done where conditions are lim- I would not advise much mixing of varieties. On the contrary, I would prefer to give over each little piece of ground to one plant. Those of low habit I would have near the path, giving the places back of them to taller-growing kinds. Of course, in the majority of small homes, there is not much chance for exercising a choice in the location of one's flowering or vegetable plants; still, it is well to study the possibilities for general effect, and do all that can be done to secure pleasing results.
passages.plain: You can do a lot even if your space is limited. More people are learning this and succeeding every year. I do not advise mixing many different types of plants together. Instead, I prefer to give each small piece of ground to one type of plant. You should put short plants near the path. You should put taller plants behind them. In most small homes, you might not have many choices for where to put your flowers or vegetables. However, you should still look at how the plants look together. Do everything you can to get a pleasing result.

passages.old: Where plants that grow to a height of three feet are grown, the best place for them"is at the rear, or along the boundary of the lot, where they will serve as a background for plants of lower habit. Children should be encouraged to take an interest in the cultivation of small gardens. They will do this if the parents are willing to help them a little at the start. Show them how to spade up the soil in spring, and how to work it over and over until it is fine and mellow.
passages.plain: Place plants that grow three feet tall at the back or along the edge of your lot. They will act as a background for shorter plants. You should encourage children to take an interest in growing small gardens. They will do this if you help them a little at the start. Show them how to spade up the soil in the spring. Show them how to work the soil over and over until it is fine and mellow.

passages.old: They will make play of this part of garden work, as it 1s as natural for a child to dig in the dirt as it is for a pig to wallow in a mud-puddle. Add some kind of fertilizer to the soil, and explain to the boys and girls that it is food for the plants that are to be. Show them how to sow seed, and tell them all you can about the processes of germination, and encourage them to watch for the appearance of the seedlings. In a short time you will have aroused in them such interest in the work they have undertaken that it will be as fascinating to them as a story, and nature will take delight in writing it out for them in daily instalments that constantly increase in interest.
passages.plain: Children will enjoy this part of the garden work. It is as natural for a child to dig in the dirt as it is for a pig to play in a mud puddle. Add fertilizer to the soil. Tell the boys and girls that the fertilizer is food for the future plants. Show them how to plant seeds. Tell them everything you know about how seeds grow. Encourage them to watch for the new seedlings to appear. Soon they will be very interested in their work. It will be as exciting to them as a story. Nature will write the story for them every day. The story will become more interesting as it continues.

passages.old: The ability to know plants and how to grow them ought to be a part of every child's education. Don't let a bit of ground go to waste. Have flowers and vegetables, even if there isn't room for more than half a dozen plants, or only one plant for that matter, for that one solitary. plant will be a great deal better than none at all.
passages.plain: You should learn about plants and how to grow them. This should be part of your education. Do not let any piece of land go to waste. Grow flowers and vegetables. Even if you only have room for six plants, you should grow them. Even if you only have room for one plant, you should grow it. Having one plant is much better than having none at all.

chapters.why: It encourages people to start small by utilizing tiny spaces and emphasizes that consistent attention is more important than large scale.

chapters.title: Leftovers

passages.old: HERE are more ways than one to secure fertilizers and fine soil for the small garden. If sward is cut from the roadside, chopped into small pieces, and stored away in some corner of the yard that is convenient to get at, and the soapsuds from wash-day are poured over it each week, it will, in a short time, if stirred frequently, become a most excellent substitute for leaf-mold. The grassroots, when decayed, will become a vegetable fertilizer which will be found extremely valuable in the culture of such plants as require a light, rich soil, especially when small.
passages.plain: There are several ways to get fertilizer and good soil for your small garden. You can cut grass from the roadside and chop it into small pieces. Store it in a corner of your yard that is easy to reach. Pour soapy water from your laundry over the grass every week. If you stir it often, it will soon become a great substitute for leaf mold. When the grass roots rot, they turn into a vegetable fertilizer. This fertilizer is very useful for growing plants that need light and rich soil, especially when those plants are small.

passages.old: Some quite artistic effects can be secured in the vegetable-garden by the exercise of a little thought. The large-leaved beet has foliage of a dark, rich crimson quite as ornamental as that of many plants used by gardeners to produce the "tropical effects" which many persons admire. When planted in the background, with fine-foliaged plants like carrot or parsley in front of it, the effect will be extremely pleasing because of the contrast of color, and also of habit. The red pepper, planted where it can show its brilliantly colored fruit against the green of some plant, will give a bit of brightness that will not fail to be appreciated by those who have a keen eye for. color-harmony.
passages.plain: You can make your vegetable garden look artistic by thinking about the layout. The large-leaved beet has dark red leaves. These leaves are just as pretty as the plants people use to create tropical looks. You should plant the beets in the background. Plant plants with fine leaves like carrots or parsley in front of them. This will look very pleasing because of the different colors and shapes. You can also plant red peppers where people can see their bright fruit against green plants. This will add a bit of brightness for people who notice how colors work together.

passages.old: It is well to plan for these touches of the artistic, even in the vegetable garden. Tomatoes are often grown on racks and trellises. Where this is done there will be no danger of the fruit's decaying, as is often the case when the plants are given no support and their branches come in contact with the ground. It is a good idea to scatter clean, aS straw under the plants after they eee to set fruit. It is also a good plan to pinch off the ends of some of the tomato-vines after the first liberal setting of fruit: This throws the strength of the plant into the development of the fruit that has set, instead of into the production of new branches which are not needed.
passages.plain: You should plan for artistic touches even in your vegetable garden. People often grow tomatoes on racks and trellises. Doing this prevents the fruit from rotting. Rot often happens when plants have no support and their branches touch the ground. You should scatter clean straw under the plants after they begin to produce fruit. You should also pinch off the ends of some tomato vines after they produce their first large amount of fruit. This moves the strength of the plant into the fruit that is already growing. It stops the plant from making new branches that you do not need.

passages.old: It also hastens the maturity of it. If the tomato is allowed to do so it will keep on growing and blooming and setting fruit throughout the entire season, and as a natural consequence much of it will be immature when frost comes. It is well to prevent this wasting of the plant's forces by shortening the main branches of it in August and September. In the chapter devoted to the mention of the best varieties of vegetables to plant, I neglected to say a good word for sage and summer savory, both of which the housewife will find very useful in seasoning soups, sausage, and other articles of food.
passages.plain: This also makes the plant mature faster. If you let the tomato continue, it will keep growing, blooming, and producing fruit all season. This means much of the fruit will be immature when the frost arrives. You should prevent the plant from wasting its energy. You can do this by shortening the main branches in August and September. In the chapter about the best vegetable varieties, I did not mention sage and summer savory. A housewife will find both very useful for seasoning soups, sausage, and other foods.

passages.old: If cut when in their prime and hung in the shade to dry, all their flavor will be retained. When perfectly dry, rub the leaves from the stalks, pulverize them well, and store in paper bags to prevent the loss of their flavor. Dill and caraway seed are often used in cookery, and, as ''variety is the spice of life,' it may be well for the housewife to grow a few plants of each. 'The writer has a very vivid recollection of grandmother's caraway cookies, and many of the present generation declare a liking for pickles flavored with dill.
passages.plain: You can keep all the flavor if you cut the plants at their peak and hang them in the shade to dry. Once they are completely dry, rub the leaves off the stalks. Crush the leaves well. Store them in paper bags so they do not lose their flavor. People often use dill and caraway seeds in cooking. Because variety is the spice of life, it is a good idea for the housewife to grow a few plants of each. The writer remembers her grandmother's caraway cookies very clearly. Many people today say they like pickles flavored with dill.

passages.old: To add to the attractive appearance of the table in winter I would advise growing a few plants of the red or purple cabbage to work up in slaws and salads. Beets are capable of giving a bit of color to the table that will be as pleasing to the eye as the taste of this vegetable is delightful to the palate. A root of parsley, potted in fall, will not only afford much material for the garnishing of the various dishes to which the housewife likes to add a touch of this kind, but it can be made the basis of a really beautiful table decoration.
passages.plain: You should grow a few red or purple cabbage plants to make your winter table look better. You can use these to make salads and slaws. Beets can also add color to your table. They look good and they taste great. You can pot a parsley root in the fall. You can use it to garnish many different dishes. You can also use it to make a beautiful decoration for the table.

passages.old: A few bright flowers thrust in among its crinkly foliage will be quite as effective as many more pretentious decorative schemes. The amateur gardener may begin work with the belief that one crop in a season is all he can expect from his garden. He will soon discover his mistake. The early radishes and the first crop of lettuce will mature before midsummer, and the ground they occupied can be planted to later varieties from which a fully developed second crop can be expected. Or other vegetables, like beets and onions, can be planted where they grew, to furnish material for the pickling season.
passages.plain: You can put a few bright flowers among the crinkly leaves. This is just as effective as many fancy decorations. You might start by thinking you can only grow one crop in a season. You will soon see that you are wrong. Early radishes and the first lettuce will be ready before midsummer. You can plant later varieties in the ground they used. You can expect a full second crop from these. You can also plant other vegetables like beets and onions in the same spots. These will provide food for the pickling season.

passages.old: After the early potatoes have been dug the ground they occupied should not be allowed to lie idle. Something can be planted there for fall use. To make the garden the greatest possible source of profit, not a foot of it should be suffered to go to waste at any time during the growing season. Radishes would be well worth growing for their beauty alone. A plate of them, nested in their own green foliage gives the breakfast-table a touch of bright color that adds the charm of beauty to the food with which it is associated.
passages.plain: Do not let the ground sit empty after you dig up the early potatoes. You can plant something there for the fall. You should not let any part of the garden go to waste during the growing season. This helps you make the most profit. Radishes are worth growing because they are beautiful. A plate of radishes with their green leaves adds bright color to the breakfast table. This adds beauty to the food.

passages.old: The writer believes in making the table as attractive in appearance as the food on it is toothsome whenever it is possible to do so. } I notice that I have overlooked the pumpkin. The oversight was unintentional, and I beg the pardon of the vegetable without which the housewife would be "'lost"' along about Thanksgiving-time. The pumpkin is out of place in the small garden because of its rampant growth, but a few plants of the New England Pie variety should be grown wherever there is room for it, to supply material for the delicious pumpkin pies most of us enjoy so much in winter.
passages.plain: You should make your garden table look as attractive as the food on it whenever you can. I forgot to mention the pumpkin. I did not mean to leave it out. I apologize to the vegetable that a housewife needs for Thanksgiving. The pumpkin does not fit well in a small garden because it grows too large. However, you should grow a few New England Pie variety plants if you have enough room. These plants provide the material for the delicious pumpkin pies that most people enjoy in the winter.

passages.old: Well-ripened specimens keep well when stored in cool, dry cellars, if placed on racks or shelves that will prevent them from coming in contact with the cold, damp cellar-bottom. If frost nips the tomato-vines before all their fruit is fully ripened, pull them up and hang them against a wall where the sun can get at them. Hang blankets over them if the nights are cold. Here they will ripen as perfectly as on the vines in the garden, and one can enjoy fresh fruit from them until the coming of very cold weather.
passages.plain: Well-ripened tomatoes stay good when you store them in cool and dry cellars. You must place them on racks or shelves. This keeps them from touching the cold and damp cellar floor. If frost damages the tomato vines before the fruit is fully ripe, pull the vines up. Hang them against a wall where the sun can reach them. Hang blankets over the fruit if the nights are cold. They will ripen as well as they would on the vines in the garden. You can enjoy fresh fruit from them until the very cold weather arrives.

passages.old: Before cold weather sets in go over the garden, be it large or small, and gather up every bit of rubbish that can be found. Pull up the dead plants and burn them. Store racks and trellises under cover for use another season. If these are properly taken eare of they will last for several years, but if left exposed to the storms of winter they will be short-lived. Dig a quantity of parsnips and salsify to be stored in the cellar for winter use. Cover the strawberry-bed with leaves or straw, spreading lightly.
passages.plain: Before the cold weather arrives, check your garden. This applies to both large and small gardens. Collect every piece of rubbish you can find. Pull up the dead plants and burn them. Put your racks and trellises under a cover for the next season. These items will last for several years if you take care of them. They will not last long if you leave them out in winter storms. Dig up a lot of parsnips and salsify. Store these in the cellar for the winter. Cover the strawberry bed with leaves or straw. Spread the covering lightly.

passages.old: Coarse litter from the barn-yard is often used for this purpose, but it is objectionable because of its containing so many weed-seeds. Many experienced gardeners advocate > plowing or spading the garden in fall. This, they claim, helps to kill the larve which insects have deposited in the soil, and it puts the ground in good working condition earlier in spring. But it will have to be gone over in spring to incorporate with it whatever fertilizer is made use of. Fresh barn-yard manure should never be used. It ought to lie for at least a season before applying it to the vegetable-garden.
passages.plain: People often use coarse litter from the barn yard for this. However, it is bad because it contains many weed seeds. Many experienced gardeners say you should plow or spade the garden in the fall. They say this helps kill insect larvae in the soil. It also makes the ground ready to work earlier in the spring. You will have to go over the ground in the spring to mix in any fertilizer you use. You must never use fresh barn yard manure. It must sit for at least one season before you put it in the vegetable garden.

passages.old: Give it a chance to ferment and kill many of the seeds that are in it. If the soil of the garden contains considerable clay, and is rather stiff in consequence, the application of coarse sand, old mortar, and coal-ashes will lighten and greatly improve it. Do not allow grass or weeds to grow on any of the unused soil in or about the garden, for insects will congregate there and make it the base from which to make their raids upon the plants you set out to grow. We are often advised to apply a dressing of salt to the asparagus-bed.
passages.plain: Let the mixture ferment. This will kill many of the seeds inside it. If your garden soil has a lot of clay and feels stiff, you can improve it. Add coarse sand, old mortar, and coal ashes to make the soil lighter. Do not let grass or weeds grow on any unused soil in or near the garden. Insects will gather there. They will use that spot as a base to attack the plants you grow. People often suggest putting a layer of salt on the asparagus bed.

passages.old: I have never been able to see that the plants received any direct benefit from it, but if it is scattered quite thickly over the ground it will prevent weeds from growing, thus benefiting the plants indirectly. Asparagus is often attacked by a sporadic growth which causes the foliage to look rusty, hence the term, dsparagus-rust. As soon as it is discovered, cut the tops and burn them. If allowed to remain the plants will likely be attacked next season, as the spores are not killed by cold. If the bugs and beetles that attack young plants of cucumber, squash, and melon do not yield promptly to the application of dry road-dust, fine coal-ashes, or land-plaster, it may be well to cover frames with fine wire netting, such as door- and windowscreens are made from, and put over the plants.
passages.plain: I have never seen plants get a direct benefit from it. However, if you spread it thickly over the ground, it stops weeds from growing. This helps the plants indirectly. Asparagus often gets a disease called asparagus-rust. This disease makes the leaves look rusty. You should cut off the tops of the plants as soon as you see it and burn them. You must do this because the spores do not die in the cold. If you leave them, the plants will likely get sick again next season. If bugs and beetles attack young cucumber, squash, or melon plants, try using dry road-dust, fine coal-ashes, or land-plaster. If the bugs do not leave after you use those items, you should cover the frames with fine wire netting. You can use the same type of wire used for door and window screens.

passages.old: Care should be taken to see that these frames fit the ground snugly, or have earth banked up about them, to prevent the enemy from crawling under. After the plants have made their third or fourth leaves the beetle will not be likely to injure them. I am often asked why writers on gardening matters never advise the use of home-grown seed. One answer to this query is this: In the ordinary garden plants stand close to one another, and the varieties we grow are almost sure to mix, by one variety being pollenized by another.
passages.plain: Make sure these frames fit the ground tightly. You should also pile earth around them. This stops enemies from crawling underneath. The beetle will likely not hurt the plants after they grow three or four leaves. People often ask me why gardening writers do not suggest using seeds you grew yourself. One reason is that garden plants grow close together. The varieties you grow will almost certainly mix. This happens because one variety is pollinated by another.

passages.old: The seed from these plants will seldom produce plants like either parent variety. Sometimes they may be equal to them in most respects, but we cannot depend on their being so. Therefore, if we desire to grow superior varieties that are of pure blood, it becomes necessary for us to procure fresh seed each season from dealers who take pains to see that there shall be no ''mixing"' among their plants. Every season some enterprising seedsman comes out with an announcement that he has developed or discovered a remarkable new variety of some standard vegetable so far superior to any other variety on the market that, as soon as its merits become fully known, it will drive all competitors out of the field.
passages.plain: Seeds from these plants rarely produce plants that look like either parent. Sometimes the new plants are equal to the parents in most ways. You cannot depend on them being equal. If you want to grow superior varieties with pure blood, you must buy fresh seeds every season. You should buy them from dealers who make sure there is no mixing among their plants. Every season, a bold seedsman announces a new variety of a standard vegetable. He claims it is much better than any other variety on the market. He says that once people know its benefits, it will push all competitors out of the market.

passages.old: Of course this new candidate for favor is offered at a fancy price, '' because the supply is limited, and the demand for it is increasing to such an extent that the entire stock will soon be sold out. Order at once, to avoid disappointment."' Don't be in a hurry to take this advice. Wait until next season. The chances are that you will hear nothing more about it. We have so many very excellent varieties now that there is no reason why we should ask for anything better. If the ''novelty" is the possessor of real merit you will be sure to hear about it later, but it is hardly likely to prove an improvement on what we already have, for it is hard to imagine anything superior to the standard varieties of vegetables that we have at present.
passages.plain: This new vegetable is sold at a high price. The supply is limited. Demand is increasing so much that the stock will sell out soon. The advertisement tells you to order right now so you do not miss out. Do not rush to follow this advice. Wait until next season. You will probably hear nothing more about it. We have many excellent varieties now. There is no reason to ask for anything better. If the new variety is actually good, you will hear about it later. It is unlikely to be better than what we already have. It is hard to imagine anything better than the standard vegetable varieties we have today.

passages.old: I would not advise purchasing seed at the general store. Some of this may be reliable, but so much of it is inferior that one cannot afford to run the risk of experimenting with it. It is the part of wisdom to purchase where you can feel sure of getting just the variety you want. , We are likely to have a few frosty nights along about the middle of September. 'Tender vegetables may be injured if not protected. But if covered with blankets or papers the danger may be tided over, and during the long period of pleasant weather that generally follows these early frosts we can get as much pleasure out of the garden as it afforded during the early fall.
passages.plain: I do not advise you to buy seeds at the general store. Some of these seeds might be good. However, many are poor quality. You cannot risk trying them. It is wise to buy seeds where you are sure you will get the exact variety you want. You will likely have a few frosty nights around the middle of September. Tender vegetables might be hurt if you do not protect them. You can avoid this danger by covering them with blankets or papers. During the long period of pleasant weather that usually follows these early frosts, you can enjoy the garden as much as you did during the early fall.

passages.old: It pays to protect. The housewife will take a great deal of delight in the preparation of piccalilli, chowchow, and the various other condiments which have such a stimulating effect on the appetite in early spring, when "'that tired feeling" is likely to make a good deal of the food that is placed before us unattractive. In the making of these good things unripe tomatoes and peppers will play an important part. So will onions that are too small to store away for winter use. She will find use for all of these things which a man would consider worthless.
passages.plain: It is worth protecting your crops. A housewife will enjoy making piccalilli, chowchow, and other condiments. These foods help stimulate the appetite in early spring. During that time, a tired feeling might make food look unattractive. Unripe tomatoes and peppers are important for making these items. Onions that are too small to store for winter are also useful. She will find a use for all of these things that a man might think are worthless.

passages.old: Really, there is but little chance for waste of garden productions if there is an appreciative and prudent woman in the kitchen. . few roots of horseradish should find a place in all gardens, preferably in some outof-the-way corner where it can be allowed to spread without interfering with other plants. Spread it will, every little piece of root that is broken off in the ground in digging the large roots becoming an independent plant as soon as thrown upon its own resources. Because of this tendency to ''take possession of the land'' many persons who have undertaken its culture refuse to give it a place in their seat But it is really an easy matter to keep it within the limits assigned it by promptly uprooting any plant that may make its appearance outside the space given over to it.
passages.plain: You can avoid wasting your garden produce if you have a smart woman in the kitchen. You should put a few horseradish roots in your garden. Put them in a corner away from other plants so they can spread. The plant will spread easily. Every small piece of root that breaks off in the ground will grow into a new plant. It will grow as soon as it has its own resources. Some people do not grow it because it tries to take over the land. However, it is easy to keep it in its own space. You just have to pull out any plant that grows outside the area you gave it.

passages.old: Those who are fond of something pungent and peppery to eat with meats, either hot or cold, will not consent to be sleet it. It is at its best as soon as the frost is out of the ground sufficiently to admit of its being dug. It should be used as soon as possible after digging, as it loses much of its piquant quality if left exposed to the air for a short time. Roots can be dug in late fall for winter use, and packed in boxes of soil, which should be stored in the cellar or some other place where they can be kept as cool as possible without actually freezing.
passages.plain: You will not like it if you want something spicy to eat with meat. It tastes best as soon as the ground is warm enough to dig it up. You should use it right after you dig it out. It loses its spicy flavor quickly if it stays in the air. You can dig the roots in late fall for the winter. You should pack them in boxes of soil. Store these boxes in a cellar or another place. Keep them as cool as possible but do not let them freeze.

passages.old: But in order to have it in perfection roots freshly dug in spring must be depended on. | Leaves of horseradish make excellent greens if used when green and tender. A few of them cooked with young beets will give the latter a flavor that will make their sweetness all the more appreciable. Speaking of greens reminds me to say that the dandelion can be cultivated to advantage in the home garden. Under cultivation it improves in sizé, and becomes a plant quite unlike the tiny, hundred-leaved specimens we dig from the roadside in spring, of which a bushel will be required in order to secure a good ''mess" for a greens-loving family, as most of such a picking will have to be discarded when it is ''looked over" preparatory to cooking.
passages.plain: To get the best results, you must use roots that are freshly dug in the spring. Horseradish leaves make great greens if you use them while they are green and tender. If you cook a few of them with young beets, the beets will taste even sweeter. You can also grow dandelions in your home garden. When you cultivate them, they grow larger. They will look very different from the tiny plants with a hundred leaves that you find on the roadside in the spring. You would need a whole bushel of those roadside plants to get enough for a family that loves greens. This is because you would have to throw away most of them after you check them before cooking.

passages.old: In order to prevent the gardengrown dandelion from becoming a nuisance it must not be allowed to bloom and develop seed. A most delightful salad can be made from the new growth of the dandelion, in spring, if properly bleached. This can be done by covering the plants with dry leaves as soon as they begin to grow, thus excluding light and inducing rapid development. Or, if most convenient, flower-pots can be inverted over the plants. The small amount of light that comes to them through the drainage-hole in the bottom of the pot will materially assist in hastening the growth of the leaves in such a manner as to give them a crisp tenderness and deprive them of. that bitter tang which characterizes the foliage when fully grown under exposure to the light and air.
passages.plain: You must not let your garden dandelions bloom or make seeds. If you do, they will become a nuisance. You can make a great salad from new dandelion growth in the spring. You must bleach the plants first. You can do this by covering the plants with dry leaves as soon as they start to grow. This blocks the light and makes them grow fast. Alternatively, you can turn flower pots upside down over the plants. A small amount of light will come through the drainage hole at the bottom of the pot. This light helps the leaves grow quickly. It makes the leaves crisp and tender. This process removes the bitter taste that leaves get when they grow fully in the light and air.

passages.old: Just enough of this spicy quality to make the salad delightfully appetizing will be found in them when grown in this way. Mention has several times been made in the preceding pages of Bordeaux mixture. This is a preparation used by smali-fruit growers everywhere to combat diseases of a fungous character which prevail to an alarming extent in almost all sections of the country in early spring. It is a standard remedy for many of the ills that this class of plants is heir to, and no up-to-date orchardist would think for a moment of neglecting its use if he would grow a fine crop of apples.
passages.plain: You will find just enough of this spicy quality to make the salad taste good when you grow them this way. The previous pages mentioned Bordeaux mixture several times. Small-fruit growers everywhere use this mixture to fight fungal diseases. These diseases appear in many parts of the country during early spring. It is a standard treatment for many problems that these plants have. No modern orchardist would skip using it if they want to grow a good crop of apples.

passages.old: It has not heretofore come into common use among those who grow small fruit on a small scale, because it 1s rather difficult to prepare it properly, but now a preparation of it that is ready for use by simply mixing it with water can be obtained from all seedsmen. The use of it in spring when fruit is setting, to prevent injury from the curculio and other enemies of small fruits, is to be encouraged. ~ Every gardener should be provided with pruning-shears with which to prune whatever plants he or she may grow that require frequent attention of that kind.
passages.plain: People who grow small fruit on a small scale have not used this much before. This is because it was hard to prepare correctly. Now you can buy a version from all seed merchants. You can use it by simply mixing it with water. You should use it in the spring when fruit is forming. This will stop damage from the curculio and other enemies of small fruits. Every gardener should have pruning shears. Use them to prune any plants you grow that need frequent pruning.

passages.old: A jack-knife answers the purpose very well in the hands of a man, but up to the present time no woman is known to have made a success of its use. Currant-bushes grow readily from cuttings. Insert a piece of half-ripened wood five or six inches long into the ground and it will almost invariably take root. In order to keep this plant in healthy bearing condition it should be pruned rather severely each season. Cut away all weak wood, and encourage the production of strong new shoots, from which fruit will be borne next season.
passages.plain: A jack-knife works well for a man. However, no woman has been known to use it successfully until now. Currant bushes grow easily from cuttings. You should put a piece of half-ripened wood into the ground. The piece should be five or six inches long. It will almost always grow roots. You must prune the plant severely every season to keep it healthy. Cut away all weak wood. You should encourage the plant to grow strong new shoots. These shoots will produce fruit next season.

passages.old: Remove a good share of the old branches after they have ripened the present season's crop. If this is not done the bush will after a little become crowded with branches, and as all branches, old and new, will attempt to bear, you will be pretty sure to have a production of very inferior fruit, since it will be impossible for the bush to perfect all the berries that set and have them come up to the standard of superiority that should govern the grower. Small currants are good, as far as they go, but the trouble is, they don't go far enough.
passages.plain: Remove a large amount of the old branches after they have ripened this season's crop. If you do not do this, the bush will soon become crowded with branches. All branches, both old and new, will try to grow fruit. You will likely get very poor fruit because the bush cannot finish growing all the berries. The berries will not reach the high standard you want. Small currants are good, but the problem is that they are not good enough.

passages.old: Many of them will have to be discarded when the housewife makes her selection. If the amateur gardener desires to give some of his vegetables an early start, I would advise him to try what may be called the '"sod-method" in Epa reac to any other. Sod is cut from roadside or pasture in fall and stacked up in the cellar for use in early spring. When seed is to be sown, invert the piece of sod, and scatter the seed over the surface, which, it will be understood, was not the surface originally.
passages.plain: The housewife will discard many of them when she chooses which ones to keep. If you want to give some of your vegetables an early start, I advise you to try the sod method. This is better than any other method. You cut sod from a roadside or a pasture in the fall. You stack it in the cellar to use in early spring. When you are ready to sow the seed, turn the piece of sod over. Scatter the seed over the surface. This surface was not the original surface.

passages.old: In other words, what was the surface is now the bottom of the piece which receives the seed. When it comes time to put the seedlings out of doors the sod can be cut apart in such a manner that each has its bit of soil, and this can be transferred to the garden without interfering in any way with the roots of the young plant. While barnyard manure, especially that which contains a good deal of cow manure, is one of the very best of all fertilizers, it is not always obtainable, and this makes it necessary to resort to some kind of commercial fertilizer.
passages.plain: The surface is now the bottom of the piece that holds the seed. When you are ready to move the seedlings outside, you can cut the sod into pieces. Each piece will have its own soil. You can move these pieces to the garden. This method will not hurt the roots of the young plants. Barnyard manure is one of the best fertilizers. It is especially good if it has a lot of cow manure. You cannot always get barnyard manure. Because of this, you must sometimes use a commercial fertilizer.

passages.old: If one is not familiar with any of these fertilizers he ought not to select at random, as he may get a kind not at all adapted to his requirements. I would advise finding some one who understands the peculiarity of the soil in his locality, and who has had some experience in the use of commercial fertilizers, and being governed by his advice. Experimental knowledge is often expensive, and the use of a fertilizer that is not adapted to the soil in one's garden often ruins a season's crops.
passages.plain: You should not pick a fertilizer at random if you do not know them. You might choose a type that does not work for your needs. You should find someone who understands the specific soil in your area. This person should have experience using commercial fertilizers. You should follow their advice. Learning through trial and error is often expensive. Using a fertilizer that does not fit your garden soil can ruin your crops for the whole season.

passages.old: The ideal support for pea-vines is brush, but not every gardener is able to obtain it. Some persons substitute binder-twine stretched from stake to stake. This answers very well as long as the weather remains dry, but as soon as a rain-storm comes along the twine absorbs so much moisture that it relaxes its tension and sags in such a manner as to endanger the vines which have taken hold of it. Coarse-meshed wire netting will be found much more satisfactory, as it will not sag and cannot be blown down by winds.
passages.plain: Brush is the best support for pea vines. However, not every gardener can get brush. Some people use binder twine stretched between stakes instead. This works well when the weather is dry. But when it rains, the twine soaks up water. The twine then loses its tension and sags. This can hurt the vines that are holding onto it. Coarse wire netting is much better. It will not sag and the wind cannot blow it down.

passages.old: Care must be taken to see that it 7s coarse-meshed, as the fine-meshed sorts will not admit of the vine's working its way out and in among the meshes. If a supply of brush can be obtained, use it by all means, and at the end of the pea-season pull it up and store it away in a dry place. If this is done, it can be made to do duty for several seasons. If netting is used, do not allow it to remain out of doors in winter. By untacking it from the stakes which are set for its support, and rolling it up carefully, and storing it away from the storms of winter, it can be made to a lifetime.
passages.plain: You must make sure the mesh is coarse. Fine mesh will not let the vine grow through the holes. Use a brush if you can get one. Pull it up at the end of the pea season and store it in a dry place. If you do this, it can last for several seasons. Do not leave netting outside during the winter. Untie the netting from the stakes that support it. Roll it up carefully. Store it away from winter storms. If you do this, it can last a lifetime.

passages.old: Don't depend upon home-grown seed. Some of it may be just as good as that which can be bought from reliable seedsmen, but the probabilities are that it is not, because of the tendencies of most plants to ''mix."' Plants grown from seed saved from the home garden often, and generally, show some of the characteristics of several varieties of the same family, and frequently these characteristics are not the ones we would like to perpetuate. Seedlings from varieties pollenized by other varieties show a decided inclination to revert to original types, and these are in most instances the very characteristics we would like to get away from.
passages.plain: Do not rely on seeds you saved from your own garden. Some of these seeds might be as good as seeds from a reliable seed seller. However, it is more likely that they are not good. This is because most plants tend to mix. Plants grown from saved seeds often show traits from several different varieties in the same family. These traits are often not the ones you want to keep. Seedlings from varieties that were pollinated by other varieties often go back to their original types. In most cases, these are the exact traits you want to get rid of.

passages.old: It is always advisable to procure fresh seed each season, and to procure it from men who make seed-growing a specialty. The housewife who likes to make her table and the food she places upon it as attractive as possible, will do well to pot a few plants of parsley in early fall. Choose for this purpose the smaller plants. Three or four can be put into one pot if the latter is of good size. These can be kept in the kitchen window, where they will be quite as ornamental as most house plants, or they can be kept in the cellar se if frost is prevented from getting to them.
passages.plain: You should always buy fresh seeds every season. Buy them from people who specialize in growing seeds. If you want your table and food to look attractive, you should pot a few parsley plants in early fall. Choose small plants for this. You can put three or four plants into one pot if the pot is large enough. You can keep these plants in a kitchen window. They will look as nice as most house plants. You can also keep them in the cellar if you keep them away from frost.

passages.old: From them one can always obtain material for the decoration of roasts and other dishes which require garnishment. Squashes and pumpkins will not keep well if stored in very warm places. A room that is just a little above the frost-point is the best place for them. It will be found far superior to a cellar, as the latter is generally more or less damp, and dampness is one of the worst enemies of these vegetables. A cool, dry atmosphere is what they need, and if it can be given them they can be kept in fine condition throughout the entire winter.
passages.plain: You can use these to decorate roasts and other dishes. Squashes and pumpkins do not stay fresh in very warm places. The best place for them is a room just slightly above the freezing point. This is much better than a cellar. Cellars are usually damp. Dampness is one of the worst enemies of these vegetables. They need a cool and dry atmosphere. If you give them this, they can stay in great condition all winter.

passages.old: Care should be taken, in gathering them, to not break their stems. If this is done they frequently decay at the place where stem and vegetable unite, and this condition spreads rapidly to all portions of them. The question is frequently asked: Would you advise plowing or spading the garden in fall? If it could have but one season's attention, | would advise giving it in spring. But if the owner of a garden has ample time to devote to it, | would advise plowing or spading in both seasons.
passages.plain: Be careful not to break the stems when you gather them. If you break them, they often rot where the stem meets the vegetable. This rot spreads quickly through the whole vegetable. People often ask if you should plow or spade the garden in the fall. If you only have time for one season, you should do it in the spring. If you have enough time, you should plow or spade the garden in both seasons.

passages.old: Turning up the soil in fall exposes to the elements that portion of it which is most likely to contain worms and insects which have burrowed away for the winter, and it is desirable to make way with as many of these as possible. Stirring the soil in spring will do them very little harm, as the weather will be in their favor. Fall stirring of the soil is also conducive to a greater degree of mellowness than is likely to result from one operation, and that in spring, as the clods of earth that are thrown up disintegrate under the influence of frost and will be in a condition to pulverize easily when spring comes.
passages.plain: Turning over the soil in the fall exposes the parts where worms and insects hide for the winter. You should try to get rid of as many of these pests as possible. Stirring the soil in the spring will not hurt them much because the weather will be good for them. Stirring the soil in the fall also makes the ground softer than stirring it just once in the spring. This happens because frost breaks up the clumps of dirt. These clumps will be easy to crush when spring arrives.

passages.old: The average gardener doesn't seem to assoclate the growing of vegetables with an idea of beauty, but he will find, if he looks into the matter, that the vegetable-garden can be made really ornamental. A row of carrots with its feathery green foliage is quite as attractive as many of our decora- ' tive plants; and beets, with crimson foliage, are really tropical in their rich coloring. Parsley and lettuce make excellent and ornamental edgings for beds containing other vegetables. Tomatoes, trained to upright trellises, are quite as showy as many kinds of flowers, when their fruit begins to ripen. - Peppers work in charmingly with the colorscheme of the vegetable-garden.
passages.plain: Most gardeners do not think growing vegetables is about beauty. However, you will find that a vegetable garden can be very decorative if you look closely. A row of carrots with feathery green leaves is just as attractive as many decorative plants. Beets have crimson leaves that look tropical because of their rich color. You can use parsley and lettuce as beautiful borders for beds that have other vegetables. Tomatoes grown on upright trellises look as showy as many types of flowers when their fruit starts to ripen. Peppers work well with the color scheme of the vegetable garden.

passages.old: A little' study of garden possibilities will soon convince one that it 1s an easy matter to make the vegetable-garden as attractive, so far as color is concerned, as the flower-garden is. And while we are at work at gardening, why not make it as attractive as possible? The pleasing appearance of it will lend additional qualities to the fine flavor of its vegetables if we believe that beauty and practicality ought to work in harmony with each other. Sage, summer savory, and other gardengrown plants used for seasoning or medicinal purposes should be gathered when in their prime.
passages.plain: A little study of garden possibilities will show you that making a vegetable garden colorful is easy. You can make it as attractive as a flower garden. You should make it as beautiful as possible while you are working on it. A pleasing appearance makes the vegetables taste even better if you believe beauty and usefulness should work together. You should gather sage, summer savory, and other plants used for seasoning or medicine when they are at their best.

passages.old: If one waits until late in the season before cutting them, much of their virtue will have been expended in the ripening process which all plants undergo after they complete their growth. Cut them close to the ground, and tie them in loose bunches, and hang them in a shady place until their moisture has evaporated. Then put them in paper bags and hang away in a store-room or closet for the winter. Plants treated in this way will retain nearly all their original flavor, and be found far superior to the kinds you buy at the store.
passages.plain: Do not wait until late in the season to cut the plants. They will lose much of their quality during the ripening process. Cut them close to the ground. Tie them in loose bunches. Hang them in a shady place until the moisture evaporates. Put them in paper bags. Hang the bags in a store room or a closet for the winter. Plants treated this way will keep almost all of their original flavor. They will be much better than the kinds you buy at the store.

passages.old: Cucumbers that have grown to full size should be gathered if not wanted for use, as to allow them to remain on the vines after reaching maturity, and while ripening, materially affects the productiveness of the plants. Endive is the basis of one of our best and most wholesome fall and winter salads. When nearly full-grown it must be bleached, like celery. Gather the leaves together and tie them in such a manner as to exclude the light. Do this when they are perfectly dry. If wet or damp they are likely to rot.
passages.plain: You should pick cucumbers when they reach full size if you do not want to use them. Leaving them on the vines after they are mature and while they ripen hurts the plants' ability to produce more fruit. Endive is the base for one of our best and healthiest fall and winter salads. You must bleach it when it is nearly full grown, just like celery. Gather the leaves together and tie them so that no light gets in. Do this when the leaves are completely dry. If they are wet or damp, they will likely rot.

passages.old: Some gardeners use what is called onion '"'sets"? instead of seed. These '"'sets" are the result of sowing seed very thickly in spring the season before they are wanted for planting. As soon as their tops die off in summer, as they will if seed was sown thickly enough, store in a dry and airy place, and the following spring replant. By this method large onions are obtained very early in the season. Most market-gardeners depend on ''sets"' instead of seed. Mention has been made of a few of our pot and medicinal plants.
passages.plain: Some gardeners use onion sets instead of seeds. These sets come from planting seeds very thickly in the spring of the previous year. When the tops of the plants die in the summer, store them in a dry and airy place. You can replant them the following spring. This method produces large onions very early in the season. Most market gardeners use sets instead of seeds. We have mentioned a few of our pot and medicinal plants.

passages.old: Here is a larger list for those who are interested in plants of this kind: balm, sweet basil, caraway, catnip, camomile, coriander, dill, pennyroyal, peppermint, saffron, tansy, and wormwood. Our grandmothers had _ unlimited faith in the medicinal qualities of some of these plants, and many a mother will be glad to know that she has a stock of some of them stored away for winter use when colds and coughs are prevalent among children or grown people. Some of the old home remedies are far preferable to those we are aceustomed to using, as they are harmless, if they do no good, which is something that cannot be said of most drugs that are taken into the system.
passages.plain: Here is a larger list for people who want to grow these plants. The list includes balm, sweet basil, caraway, catnip, chamomile, coriander, dill, pennyroyal, peppermint, saffron, tansy, and wormwood. Our grandmothers had great faith in the medicinal qualities of some of these plants. Many mothers will be happy to have a stock of these plants stored for the winter. You can use them when children or adults have colds and coughs. Some old home remedies are better than the ones we use today. They are harmless even if they do not work. You cannot say the same thing about most drugs that people take into their bodies.

passages.old: Don't wait for the currant-worm to show itself on your bushes. You can safely count on its coming. Act on the defensive in advance by spraying your plants thoroughly with an infusion of Nicoticide, keeping in mind the fact that it is easier to prevent an insect from establishing itself on your plants than it is to get rid of it when it has secured a foothold there. In spraying, be sure that the infusion gets to all parts of the bush. Throw it up well among the branches. Simply spraying it over the plant isn't what is needed.
passages.plain: Do not wait for the currant-worm to appear on your bushes. You can be sure it will come. Take defensive action early by spraying your plants thoroughly with a Nicoticide infusion. It is easier to stop an insect from starting on your plants than it is to remove it once it has settled there. Make sure the infusion reaches all parts of the bush when you spray. Throw it up well among the branches. You do not need to simply spray it over the plant.

warnings.text: This passage names an old pest poison or spray. Some of these are banned now, and none should be mixed at home. Use only a product sold for home gardens today, and follow its label.
